senses.definition: (rare) One who abnegates, denies, or rejects.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who renounces, denies, or gives up something, such as a right, a claim, or a pleasure.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AB, and the final syllable is an American r-colored 'er' sound. Non-native speakers often stress the wrong syllable or pronounce the last syllable as a full 'tor.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to admirable. It names someone who gives up something, which can be seen as noble or self-denying depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Abnegator is rare and mostly appears in formal writing or literary analysis. Americans seldom use it in speech. For everyday talk, you would say someone who gave something up or who refused a privilege.

distinctions.note: An ascetic lives a life of deliberate austerity as a whole. An abnegator may give up a specific right or claim without living an austere lifestyle.
Renouncer is a more general and more common word for someone who gives up a position, belief, or possession. Abnegator is more formal and focuses on the denial of self.

examples.professional: As an abnegator of executive privilege, the director insisted the team own the roadmap.
examples.analytical: The abnegator in the novel becomes a kind of moral mirror, exposing the self-interest of those who claim the same rights.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who hands back the keys to a car they could still drive.
nuance.etymology: Formed from abnegate plus the agent suffix -or, from Latin -ator, 'one who does'.
common_mistakes: Using abnegator for the act itself; the act is abnegation.
Confusing it with negator or negotiator, which have different meanings.
Forgetting the r-colored final syllable, which should sound like 'er' in American English.

senses.definition: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.
senses.example: Blackberries are abundant in this part of the country in October, so we always make lots of jam.

senses.definition: Richly supplied; wealthy; possessing in great quantity.
Being an abundant number, i.e. less than the sum of all of its divisors except itself.

core.definition: Existing or available in large amounts, more than enough; plentiful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -BUN-, with a short 'u' as in 'cup.' The last two syllables are reduced, so 'dunt' sounds like 'dent' with a weak vowel. Avoid saying 'ah-bun-DANT.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests generosity, sufficiency, or richness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'abundant' in writing, speeches, and formal descriptions, such as 'abundant rain' or 'abundant parking.' In casual speech they more often say 'plenty of' or 'lots of.' The adjective is often followed by 'in' with a noun, as in 'abundant in resources.'

distinctions.note: 'Plenty' is the everyday, informal word, while 'abundant' sounds more formal and written.
'Ample' means enough or more than enough and often refers to space or time, while 'abundant' stresses a large quantity.
'Copious' is more formal and often describes things like notes, rain, or flowing liquids.

examples.everyday: There's abundant parking at the mall on Sundays, so we don't have to worry about it.
examples.professional: We have abundant data for the churn model, so sample size shouldn't be the constraint.
examples.analytical: The manuscript offers abundant evidence that the early church read these letters as authoritative.

nuance.analogy: Like a well that never runs dry, no matter how much water is drawn from it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abundare 'to overflow,' from ab 'from' and undare 'to surge,' from unda 'wave.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (uh-bun-DANT) instead of the second.
Writing 'abundant of' instead of 'abundant in' or simply using the noun 'abundance of.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture 'abundant' translates Greek words meaning overflowing or superabundant, from perisseuō 'to abound, overflow.' John 10:10 says Jesus came that people may have life and have it abundantly, a verse often read as the fullness of life in him. Romans 5:20 says that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, and 2 Corinthians 9:8 says God is able to make all grace abound toward believers.

senses.definition: Something to be added; especially text added as an appendix or supplement to a document.
senses.example: An addendum was added to the contract to clarify payment terms.

senses.definition: A postscript.
The height by which the tooth of a gear projects beyond (outside for external, or inside for internal) the standard pitch circle or pitch line.

core.definition: Something added to the end of a document, such as an appendix, supplement, or extra note that completes it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, DEN, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'dum' rather than 'doom'. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical addition to a document and carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use addendum mostly in business, legal, academic, and technical writing, such as a contract addendum or a report addendum. In everyday speech, people usually say 'extra page' or 'update' instead. The plural is addenda, though 'addendums' is also accepted in American business writing.

distinctions.note: An appendix is usually at the back of a book and is part of the original plan, while an addendum is added later to update or correct the document.
A supplement adds material to extend a publication, while an addendum is usually shorter and tied to a specific correction or change.

examples.everyday: Hey, I added a quick addendum to the lease, so check the last page before you sign.
examples.professional: I've attached an addendum to the project proposal that covers the revised budget and timeline.
examples.analytical: The author's addendum modifies the original argument by acknowledging the limitations of the sample.

nuance.analogy: An addendum is like a sticky note added to the bottom of a printed page with a new fact you forgot to include.
nuance.etymology: From Latin addendum, 'something to be added,' the neuter gerundive of addere, 'to add.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AD-en-dum.
Using addendum for a plural set of additions without changing it to addenda.

senses.definition: Receiving others kindly and conversing with them in a free and friendly manner; friendly, courteous, sociable.
Mild; benign.

core.definition: Friendly, warm and easy to talk to, putting people at ease in conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the last two syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like buhl. Do not add an extra syllable such as af-ah-bull.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a warm, approachable person and sounds polished rather than casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use affable more in writing, reviews and news than in everyday speech. In conversation they might say nice or easy to talk to instead. Calling a host, doctor or coworker affable is a compliment that signals warmth with some polish.

distinctions.note: Friendly is the everyday word for warmth; affable suggests a relaxed, sociable manner that puts others at ease.
Amiable focuses on a pleasant, good-natured disposition; affable adds the idea of being easy to talk to.

examples.everyday: The guy at the hardware store was really affable and walked me straight to the right aisle.
examples.professional: Our new account manager is affable on calls, so clients tend to stay longer and share more about their needs.
examples.analytical: A good interlocutor is affable without being servile, giving others room to speak while keeping the argument honest.

nuance.analogy: An affable person is like a comfortable sofa: approachable and easy to settle into.
nuance.etymology: From Latin affabilis, easy to address, from affari, to speak to.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in af-AH-bul.
Using affable for someone who was nice for a single moment; it describes a steady, pleasant manner.

affable.etymology: French *affable*, from Latin *affābilis*, from *affor* (“to address”), from *ad* + *for* (“to speak, to talk”).

senses.definition: Of, or relating to, the ownership, tenure and cultivation of land.
Agricultural or rural.
Wild; said of plants growing in a cultivated field.
A person who advocates the political interests of working farmers.

core.definition: Relating to farming, farmland, or land ownership, especially in a rural society where farming is the main economic activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, GRAIR, which sounds like 'air' with an r. The final syllable is a reduced 'ee-un,' so do not say 'ah-GRAIR-ee-an' with an open a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an economic or social system without clear praise or criticism, though it can carry political meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use agrarian mainly in history, economics, and political discussions about rural life or land policy. In everyday talk, 'farm' or 'rural' is more natural. For farming activity itself, 'agricultural' is the usual word, while agrarian often refers to a whole way of life or a political ideal. A natural reply is to ask about the time period or the policy being discussed.

distinctions.note: Agricultural describes farming activities and methods, while agrarian describes a society, economy, or political ideal centered on land and farming.
Rural means related to the countryside in general, while agrarian focuses on land cultivation and farmers as an economic or political class.

examples.everyday: My grandparents grew up in an agrarian town where almost everyone grew something in their backyard.
examples.professional: The policy team is reviewing how drought insurance affects small farms in our agrarian regions.
examples.analytical: Jefferson's vision of a republic of independent farmers rested on an agrarian ideal in which land ownership supported civic virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a town built around its river, with its whole economy and identity shaped by the land beneath it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin agrarius, 'of fields,' from ager, 'field.'
common_mistakes: Using agrarian for any farming activity, when agricultural is the usual word for farming methods.
Pronouncing it with a full open vowel, as in 'ah-GRAIR-ee-an,' instead of the reduced final syllable.

agrarian.etymology: From Middle French *agrarien*, from Latin *agrarius* (“of the land”), from stem of *ager* (“field”) + *-arius*.

senses.definition: Cold, chilly; used of low body temperature, especially in connection with certain diseases such as malaria and cholera.
senses.example: algid malaria

core.definition: Very cold, chilly, especially describing a low body temperature during illness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'g' as a 'j' sound, like 'jump'. The final 'id' is short, rhyming with 'rid' or 'kid'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical. It describes an unpleasant cold, often in a medical context, and it sounds formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'algid' in conversation; it belongs to medical history and older literary writing. A doctor might describe a patient as algid in a historical or pathology context. In everyday talk, say 'chilled' or 'freezing'.

distinctions.note: Chilly is ordinary and mild; algid is formal and suggests a clinically dangerous low temperature.
Frigid can describe weather or a cold personality; algid is limited to physical cold, often of the body.

examples.professional: The clinical report described the patient as algid, which told the team the infection had reached a critical stage.
examples.analytical: Historical accounts of cholera describe the algid phase, in which the body loses heat and the skin turns clammy and blue.

nuance.analogy: If a fever is a furnace running too hot, algid is the furnace gone cold, with the body losing heat it cannot replace.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'algidus', meaning 'cold', from 'algere', 'to be cold'.
common_mistakes: Using 'algid' for ordinary cold weather; it is too clinical for everyday use.
Confusing it with 'acid' because of the similar spelling; the words are unrelated.

senses.definition: To reduce or lessen the severity of a pain or difficulty.
senses.example: alleviate his pain

senses.definition: To pay down partially.
senses.example: There are different ways to alleviate your financial debt.

core.definition: To make pain, suffering or a problem less severe or easier to bear, though not always to remove it completely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LEE. The middle vowels are reduced to ih and uh, and the final -ate is ayt, not it.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying relief or improvement; it appears in medical, political and everyday contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alleviate in formal writing, medical settings and news, as in the medication alleviates pain. In casual speech they say ease, help with or make it better, so alleviate sounds a little formal. In a meeting you might say This should help alleviate some of the pressure. A natural reply is Thanks, that really helps.

distinctions.note: Relieve is more common and everyday; alleviate is more formal and often refers to lessening a condition.
Cure means to end an illness completely; alleviate only makes it less severe.
Ease is informal and gentle; alleviate is precise and formal.

examples.everyday: Try some honey tea; it might help alleviate that scratchy throat.
examples.professional: Adding a second on-call engineer should alleviate the pressure on the incident rotation.
examples.analytical: Theodicy asks whether suffering can be alleviated by God's presence without being explained away.

nuance.analogy: Like loosening a tight knot: the knot remains, but it no longer pinches.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alleviare 'to lighten', from ad 'to' and levis 'light'.
common_mistakes: Using alleviate to mean completely remove; it means make less severe
Stressing the last syllable as uh-lee-VAYT

alleviate.etymology: Late Latin *alleviatus*, past participle of *allevio* (“to lighten; to alleviate”).

senses.definition: The juice from chewing tobacco.

core.definition: The brown liquid released when someone chews tobacco and spits it out.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er', like the end of 'water'. Don't pronounce it 'am-BEER'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and crude. It describes something unpleasant and is considered dated.
nuance.usage_note: This word is archaic and mainly appears in older American fiction or in dialect writing about rural life. Today people say 'tobacco juice' or 'chew spit' in ordinary speech. It is not suitable for polite conversation, and most listeners would not recognize it.

distinctions.note: The chew is the plug of tobacco itself, while ambeer is the liquid it releases.

examples.professional: Workplace safety training covers the hygiene and health risks of spitting tobacco juice.
examples.analytical: The novel's references to ambeer mark its rural characters as coarse and outside polite society.

nuance.analogy: Like an old-fashioned word for a brown stain, one that people no longer use but still find in old books.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'amber', the golden-brown color or fossil resin.
Pronouncing it 'am-BEER' with the stress on the second syllable.

ambeer.etymology: Alteration of *amber*, due to its colour.

senses.definition: A view in Christian eschatology that rejects the claimed future thousand-year physical reign of Jesus Christ on the earth, in opposition to premillennial and some postmillennial views of the Book of Revelation, chapter 20, claiming instead that the number of years in Revelation 20 is a symbolic number and that Christ's eventual physical reign will be permanent.

core.definition: The view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 are symbolic, not a future earthly reign, and that Christ's reign is now.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEN, with secondary stress on 'ay.' The prefix a- is pronounced 'ay,' like the letter A, and not 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is a label for a position, and the name can mislead since it does not deny the Millennium entirely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in theology, especially among Reformed, Lutheran, and Catholic scholars. The 'a-' prefix means 'no,' but amillennialists do accept a millennium, interpreted spiritually. It is often explained in contrast with premillennialism and postmillennialism.

distinctions.note: 'Premillennialism' expects a literal thousand-year reign after Christ returns, but amillennialism reads the thousand years as symbolic of the present age.
'Postmillennialism' expects a coming golden age before Christ returns, whereas amillennialism does not expect such an era.
'Realized millennialism' is another name for amillennialism, stressing that the Millennium is already present in the Church.

examples.everyday: I grew up Lutheran, so I guess I was taught amillennialism without ever hearing the word.
examples.professional: The commentary explains why many Reformed scholars favor amillennialism in reading Revelation 20.
examples.analytical: Amillennialism treats the thousand years as a symbol of the present age between Christ's resurrection and his return, so Christ reigns now.

nuance.analogy: The thousand years are like a symbol for the whole church age, not a separate calendar chapter.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a-, 'not, without' + Latin millennium + -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the a- as 'uh' instead of 'ay.'
Thinking it denies any Millennium at all.
Stressing the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Amillennialists read Revelation 20:1-6 as symbolic, seeing the binding of Satan as the effect of Christ's first coming, as in Matthew 12:29, where Jesus speaks of binding the strong man. They also read the first resurrection as spiritual life with Christ, and note that John 5:28-29 speaks of one general resurrection at the last hour.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology is generally close to an amillennial reading, seeing Christ's reign as present in the Church, though it does not use that label as a formal doctrine.
Catholic teaching, following Augustine, traditionally treats the thousand years symbolically as the age of the Church, and is commonly described as amillennial in effect.

Amillennialism is held by Lutherans, many Reformed Christians, and many Anglicans, who follow Augustine in reading the thousand years as symbolic. Many Baptists and Pentecostals instead hold premillennial views.

senses.definition: The measure of the size of something, especially its width or breadth; largeness, magnitude.
The maximum absolute value of the vertical component of a curve or function, especially one that is periodic.
The horizontal line which measures the distance to which a projectile is thrown; the range.
The range of motion of the gymnast's body while performing a skill.
The range of environmental conditions in which an organism can survive.
The maximum absolute value of some quantity that varies.

The arc of the horizon between the true east or west point and the center of the sun, or a star, at its rising or setting. At the rising, the amplitude is eastern or ortive: at the setting, it is western, occiduous, or occasive. It is also northern or southern, when north or south of the equator.
The arc of the horizon between the true east or west point and the foot of the vertical circle passing through any star or object.

core.definition: In mathematics and physics, the maximum displacement of a periodic wave or oscillation from its resting or average value.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on the final syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, and the ending is 'tood' in General American, not the 'tyood' of British speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical measurement term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use amplitude in science, engineering, music and math classes, and in discussions of sound volume or earthquakes. In everyday speech they say 'volume,' 'loudness' or 'size of the wave' instead. The general sense of 'breadth' or 'largeness' is old-fashioned and rarely heard in the US today.

distinctions.note: Amplitude is how big each wave swing is. Frequency is how often the wave repeats per second, so the two are independent.
Magnitude is a general measure of size or strength. Amplitude refers specifically to the maximum displacement of an oscillation or wave.
Altitude is height above sea level. The two words look similar but have completely different meanings.

examples.everyday: When you turn the volume knob up, you're making the amplitude of the sound wave bigger, so it sounds louder.
examples.professional: The sensor's noise floor hides small amplitude changes, so we need to filter the signal before we model the vibration.
examples.analytical: Reducing the amplitude of a pendulum's swing does not change its period, which is why its frequency stays constant even as it slows.

nuance.analogy: Like how far a child's swing goes up and down from the middle: that distance is the amplitude.
nuance.etymology: From Latin amplitudo, 'largeness, breadth,' from amplus 'large.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'altitude,' which is height above sea level.
Saying 'AM-plih-TYOOD,' the British-style ending, instead of the American 'tood.'
Using it in everyday speech where 'volume' or 'loudness' is more natural.

amplitude.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *amplitude*, from Latin *amplitūdō*, from *amplus* (“large”).

senses.definition: That follows necessarily by definition; tautologous.
Of, or relating to algebra or a similar method of analysis.
Being defined in terms of objects of differential calculus such as derivatives.
Being able to be locally represented by convergent power series around every point of the domain.
Of, or relating to any form of analysis, or to analytics.
senses.example: analytic method

senses.definition: Of, or relating to division into elements or principles.
Having the ability to analyze.
Of a language, having a grammar principally dependent on the arrangement of uninflected function words within sentences to indicate meaning.
A proposed role for each of a society's components.
senses.example: It is tempting to take the case of Islamic traditions as instances of such a counterpublic and generalize this into an analytic of Islamic traditions and modernity tout court. ~Brian Silverstein, Islam and Modernity in Turkey (2010), Palgrave Macmillan, ISBN 978-0-230-10982-7, p. 2.

core.definition: Relying on logical analysis; in philosophy, true by the meaning of its words alone, without checking the world.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, LIT, with a light secondary stress on AN. The middle syllables are reduced to uh and a short i, not 'uh-NAL-ih-tik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. Describing a person as analytic is mildly positive, suggesting careful, logical thinking.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say 'analytical' for a person who breaks problems down carefully, as in 'She's very analytical'. 'Analytic' is more typical in technical or academic contexts, such as 'analytic philosophy', 'analytic function' or 'analytic geometry'. In a meeting, you can use either, but 'analytical' is the safer everyday choice.

distinctions.note: Analytic is more technical and appears in set phrases like 'analytic philosophy', while analytical is the everyday word for a person's careful thinking style.
In philosophy, an analytic statement is true by definition, while a synthetic statement depends on facts about the world.
Logical is broader and describes any sound reasoning, while analytic is specific to truth that follows from definitions or to breaking things into parts.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor says 'all bachelors are unmarried' is analytic, so you don't need to check the world to know it's true.
examples.professional: Let's take an analytic approach to the churn problem and break it into measurable drivers before we pick a model.
examples.analytical: Kant's distinction between analytic and synthetic judgments asks whether the predicate is already contained in the concept of the subject.

nuance.analogy: An analytic truth is like a dictionary definition that cannot be wrong, because its truth comes from the words themselves.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'analytikos', 'able to resolve', from 'analyein', 'to unloose or resolve'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'She is analytic' for a person's thinking style. Americans normally say 'She is analytical'.
Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, as in 'uh-NAL-ih-tik'. The stress falls on LIT.

senses.definition: That appeals to, or stimulates the appetite.
senses.example: This food looks so appetizing.

senses.definition: Appealing or enticing.
Any food traditionally eaten with a bagel, as an accompaniment, topping or filling; including dairy products and pareve but not meat.

core.definition: Looking, smelling, or sounding so good that it makes you want to eat it, or figuratively attractive and enticing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a weak schwa in the middle, so it is 'AP-uh-ty-zing,' not 'ap-ih-TIZE-ing.' The final '-ing' is a clear 'ng' sound with no 'n' alone.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a polite, somewhat formal word for food that looks or smells good.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That looks good' or 'That smells delicious' most often, so appetizing sounds a bit more formal or written. In New York, an 'appetizing store' is a Jewish-American shop that sells smoked fish, cream cheese, and bagel accompaniments, so the word has a local meaning there. Figuratively, you can say 'an appetizing offer' or 'an appetizing deal' in business talk.

distinctions.note: Delicious describes taste after you eat, while appetizing describes appearance or smell before you eat.
Mouthwatering is more vivid and enthusiastic, suggesting something that makes your mouth water.
Tasty is casual and focuses on flavor, while appetizing is more about how food looks or smells.

examples.everyday: Wow, that pizza smells appetizing, so let's order it.
examples.professional: The redesigned dashboard looks more appetizing, so people actually open it, but the underlying numbers still need work.
examples.analytical: Hume suggests that what seems appetizing to one judge may depend on the cultivated judgment of the perceiver.

nuance.analogy: Like a bakery window, the display makes you want to walk in before you know what is inside.
nuance.etymology: From appetize, from French appétiser, from appétit 'appetite.'
common_mistakes: Using appetizing for taste after eating; say 'delicious' or 'tasty' for flavor.
Confusing the adjective with the noun appetizer; 'The food looks appetizing' is correct, not 'The food looks appetizer.'

conversation.text: The food didn't look very appetizing, but it tasted great.
Adding some green herbs makes the plate more appetizing.
That gray soup is not very appetizing.

senses.definition: The object of somebody's affections; a person (or sometimes a thing) that someone strongly prefers; a favorite, a loved one.
senses.example: Sara was never the same after losing her daughter, the apple of her eye.

core.definition: Someone you love and prefer above everyone else, especially a child or grandchild, or sometimes something you treasure greatly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress APPLE and EYE, while 'of' and 'my' are weak and reduced, so the phrase sounds like 'AP-uhl-uhv-my-EYE.' The word 'apple' has a syllabic l, so the last syllable is not a separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Warm, affectionate, and sentimental. It can sound old-fashioned, so people often use it with a smile.
nuance.usage_note: Parents, grandparents, and older relatives use this phrase most often, as in 'My granddaughter is the apple of my eye.' Use the possessive that matches the person you mean, such as 'the apple of his eye,' and do not use it for casual crushes. A natural reply is 'Aw, that's sweet' or 'I know, she's adorable.'

distinctions.note: Darling is a term of address, while the apple of my eye describes someone you favor above others.
Favorite is neutral and can describe things or people, but the apple of my eye is warmer and usually refers to a beloved person.
Teacher's pet is often negative, describing someone who gets special treatment, while the apple of my eye is affectionate.

collocations: be the apple of someone's eye
always the apple of Dad's eye

examples.everyday: Ruth's grandson is the apple of her eye, and she brags about him constantly.
examples.professional: Our CEO treats the customer success team like the apple of her eye, so they always get the budget they ask for.
examples.analytical: Lear's favor shifts from Cordelia to her sisters, which shows how fragile it can be to be the apple of someone's eye.

nuance.analogy: Like the pupil of the eye, it is the small center you protect without thinking.
nuance.etymology: Originally referred to the pupil of the eye, and the figurative sense of a cherished person developed from that.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong possessive, as in 'the apple of my eye' when you mean 'the apple of his eye' about someone else.
Using the phrase for casual crushes or for everyday favorites like pizza; it is strongly affectionate and is mainly used for people.

apple-of-my-eye.etymology: From Middle English *appel of the eie* (“pupil of the eye; cornea; something highly valued”), from Old English *æppel on the ēagan*, used in biblical texts (Deuteronomy 32:10, Psalm 17:8; Proverbs 7:2, Lamentations 2:18, and Zechariah 2:8; compare the…

conversation.text: My little granddaughter is the apple of my eye.
"You really love that dog, huh?" "Are you kidding? Max is the apple of my eye."
Since the day she was born, my daughter has been the apple of my eye.

senses.definition: In an apposite manner.

core.definition: In a way that is suitable, fitting, or relevant to the situation or point being made.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -ly is a clear, unstressed 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a remark, quotation, or example as well chosen, and it is neutral in tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing and formal speech, such as academic work, legal commentary, or professional reports. In everyday talk, people say 'appropriately' or 'fittingly' instead. It sounds showy in casual conversation but is natural in an essay or a presentation.

distinctions.note: 'Appropriately' is general and everyday; 'appositely' specifically suggests an example or remark that fits the point at hand very well.
'Aptly' often implies a neat or witty fit; 'appositely' is more formal and emphasizes relevance.

examples.everyday: Dad quoted a Yogi Berra line, and he actually used it appositely for once.
examples.professional: In the review, the analyst cited the Q3 churn figures appositely to support her argument about pricing.
examples.analytical: Kant's distinction between phenomena and noumena is invoked appositely when the critic discusses the limits of knowledge.

nuance.etymology: From Latin appositus, past participle of apponere, 'to place near'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'apposite' with 'opposite'; 'apposite' means fitting, not contrary.
Using it to describe a person's character; say 'appropriate' or 'fitting' for behavior.

senses.definition: A sea or other body of water with many islands.
A group of many islands.
A thing comprising many other scattered things.
senses.example: the Gulag Archipelago

senses.definition: A cross-game modification system that randomizes in-game abilities and items scattered across multiple and different modded games.
(rare) To scatter or strew (a place, or something) with things that collectively resemble a group of many islands.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A group of many islands, or a body of water containing many scattered islands.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on PEL, the second syllable, and the first syllable has a light secondary stress. The final syllable goh rhymes with go.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often describes scenic places and travel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use archipelago in geography, travel writing, and news, as in the Hawaiian archipelago. In everyday speech people more often say a chain of islands or a group of islands. Place names often capitalize the word, and it can also be used figuratively for a scattered set of things.

distinctions.note: An island chain is usually a line of islands in a row, while an archipelago is a more general group of scattered islands.
Island group is a plain everyday phrase, while archipelago sounds more formal and geographic.

examples.everyday: We took a boat tour around the archipelago, and the water was so clear.
examples.professional: Shipping to the archipelago by sea adds two days to our delivery schedule.
examples.analytical: Writers often use an archipelago as a metaphor for isolated communities that are connected only by the sea.

nuance.analogy: Like a scatter of stepping stones across a pond, but on a much larger scale.
nuance.etymology: From Italian arcipelago, from Greek Aigaion pelagos 'Aegean Sea', later applied to any group of islands.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on PEL.
Spelling it archipelego with an e instead of an a.

archipelago.etymology: The is Italian *arcipelago* (“Aegean Sea; group of many islands”), from *arci-* (variant of *archi-*) + *pelago* (“ sea”):

senses.definition: On the land as opposed to onboard.
On, or towards the shore.
senses.example: The canoe sailed ashore.

core.definition: On or onto the land, having come from a ship, boat or the sea; reaching the shore.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the first vowel is a weak schwa. The r is pronounced clearly in American English, so do not drop it as in British speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ashore' mainly for travel by sea, such as sailors going ashore at a port, a cruise passenger going ashore for a few hours, or a rescue crew bringing people ashore. In everyday talk it often appears in phrases like 'go ashore' or 'come ashore.' It sounds slightly literary when used for something other than ships, so do not use it for a person simply walking to the beach.

distinctions.note: 'Ashore' describes motion or position on land after a sea journey, while 'on shore' is a more neutral location and is also used for things like 'on shore winds.'
'Onshore' describes winds or movement toward the land from the sea, and it is not used to mean having come off a ship.

examples.everyday: We had a few hours in port, so we went ashore and walked around the old harbor town.
examples.professional: The shipping report says the cargo was unloaded and taken ashore before the storm arrived.
examples.analytical: In Acts 27, the shipwrecked travelers swim or float ashore, a detail that shows how the narrative moves from danger at sea to safety on land.

nuance.analogy: A ship is like a home on the water, and 'ashore' is the moment you step back into the house on dry land.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'a shore', meaning 'on the shore', from 'a' (on) and 'shore' (the coast).
common_mistakes: Using 'ashore' for a location that is not on land after a voyage, such as a person standing by a lake, where 'at the shore' or 'by the lake' is more natural.
Confusing 'ashore' with 'onshore' when talking about winds or movement toward the coast.
nuance.biblical_note: The English idea of reaching land after a voyage corresponds to Greek phrases meaning 'to land' (epi tēn gēn, literally 'upon the land'). Luke 5:11 says the disciples brought their boats to land and left everything to follow Jesus. Acts 27:44 describes the shipwrecked company escaping to land, and Acts 27:43 has the centurion order those who could swim to jump overboard and make for land.

senses.definition: To lessen the intensity of, to mitigate or relieve (hunger, emotion, pain, etc.).
To pacify or soothe (someone).

core.definition: To make a painful feeling, need, or worry less intense, or to relieve and soothe it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SWAYJ, the second syllable. The vowel is the diphthong of 'way', and the ending is the 'j' sound of 'age', not a 'zh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests gentle, compassionate relief of pain, hunger, guilt or fear, and it sounds formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assuage mostly in writing, news reports and serious discussions of grief, guilt, anger or fear, as in 'to assuage concerns'. In everyday conversation people say 'ease', 'calm down' or 'make someone feel better'. Saying 'I assuaged my hunger with a cracker' sounds deliberately literary and may seem stiff.

distinctions.note: Ease is common and neutral. Assuage is more formal and stresses reducing a strong feeling such as grief or guilt.
Soothe is used in everyday speech for people, nerves or skin. Assuage sounds more formal and often takes abstract objects like fears or guilt.
Alleviate is more clinical and is often used for pain, symptoms or suffering in medical or policy contexts.

examples.everyday: A cup of coffee didn't quite assuage my hunger, so we grabbed a burrito on the way home.
examples.professional: The CEO's town hall was meant to assuage employee concerns about the layoffs.
examples.analytical: For many theologians, confession is a way to assuage the guilt that comes with sin.

nuance.analogy: Like pouring cool water on a burn: the heat doesn't disappear, but it becomes gentler.
nuance.etymology: From Old French assuagier, from Late Latin assuaviare 'to make gentle or sweet', from ad- plus suavis 'sweet'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it assuge or assauge. The correct spelling is assuage, with 'ua' after the 's'.
Pronouncing the ending like the 'zh' in beige instead of the 'j' in age.

assuage.etymology: From Middle English *aswagen*, from Old French *asuagier* (“to appease, to calm”), from Vulgar Latin **assuāviō* (“to sweeten, to butter up, to calm”), derived from Latin *ad-* + *suāvis* (“sweet”) + *-iō*.

senses.definition: Amazed; surprised.
senses.example: utterly astonished

core.definition: Very surprised, so much that you cannot quickly react or believe what you see or hear.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STAH, the second syllable, with the open ah vowel of 'father'. The -ed ending is a quiet t after the sh, so the word ends with 'isht', not 'ishd'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral when it describes wonder, and negative when it describes shock at something bad. It is stronger than surprised.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use astonished in everyday speech and writing for strong surprise, often as 'I was astonished that' or 'I was astonished to see'. In casual talk people more often say 'I was so surprised' or 'I couldn't believe it.' Astonished sounds more emphatic, so it fits stories, reviews and reports well.

distinctions.note: Surprised is the everyday neutral term. Astonished is much stronger and can leave you speechless.
Amazed is usually positive and impressed. Astonished can be positive or shocked, and it often sounds more intense.

examples.everyday: I was astonished when the waiter said the whole dinner was on the house.
examples.professional: The team was astonished when the model's accuracy jumped twenty points after the fix.
examples.analytical: Readers of Hume are often astonished at how little experience supports our confident beliefs about cause and effect.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden flash of lightning in a dark room: it stops you for a moment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin attonare 'to stun with thunder', from ad- 'to' plus tonare 'to thunder'.
common_mistakes: Using astonished with of, as in 'astonished of'. Use astonished by, at, or that.
Pronouncing it with a d sound, as in 'uh-STAH-nishd', instead of the final t.

conversation.text: I was astonished at how cheap the flights were.
The doctors were astonished by how quickly he recovered.
She looked astonished when everyone yelled, "Surprise!"

senses.definition: One who attends; one who works with or watches over someone or something.
senses.example: Give your keys to the parking attendants and they will park your car for you.

senses.definition: A servant or valet.
That which accompanies or follows.
One who owes a duty or service to another.
Going with; associated; concomitant.
senses.example: They promoted him to supervisor, with all the attendant responsibilities and privileges.

senses.definition: Depending on, or owing duty or service to.
senses.example: the widow attendant to the heir

core.definition: A person whose job is to serve, help or watch over people or a place, such as a flight attendant or parking attendant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TEN. The first and last syllables are weak schwas, so the word has a soft, quick final -dunt rather than a clear -dant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a service role, and it is polite to call someone an attendant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear attendant in job titles such as flight attendant, parking attendant or gas station attendant. The word is useful for describing someone who works a service counter or booth. As an adjective it sounds formal or written, as in attendant risks. A natural reply when an attendant helps you is Thanks so much!

distinctions.note: An attendee is someone who attends an event such as a conference or wedding, while an attendant works in a service role or accompanies someone.
An assistant helps someone with work tasks, while an attendant usually watches over a place or serves people in a service job.

examples.everyday: Excuse me, could you ask the attendant at the front desk where the restroom is?
examples.professional: The parking attendant logs each exit, so we can match the gate data against the badge records each morning.
examples.analytical: The attendant effects of the policy, such as higher costs for small firms, were predictable but rarely discussed in the debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a stagehand who never takes a bow but keeps the show running smoothly.
nuance.etymology: From Old French atendant, the present participle of atendre, to attend, from Latin attendere.
common_mistakes: Confusing attendant with attendee; an attendee goes to an event, while an attendant serves or watches over people or places.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ah-TEN-dant; the stress is on the second syllable, uh-TEN-dunt.

attendant.etymology: From Middle English *attendant,attendaunt*, from Old French *attendant*.

senses.definition: Indicating position or direction.
senses.example: The silt collects in the backward part of the tank.

senses.definition: Situated toward or at the rear of something.
senses.example: The silt collects in the backward part of the tank.

senses.definition: Acting or moving in the direction opposite to that in which someone or something is facing.
senses.example: a backward tilt of the head

senses.definition: Acting or moving in the direction opposite to the usual direction of movement.
senses.example: The occasional apparent backward movement of planets is evidence that they revolve around the sun.

senses.definition: Acting or moving oppositely to the desired direction of progress.
senses.example: This is a backward step for the country.

senses.definition: Reversed in order or sequence.
senses.example: This backward writing is hard to read.

senses.definition: Expressing lack of development or advancement.
senses.example: The child is backward in his school work.

senses.definition: Retarded in development; not as advanced as would be expected.
senses.example: The child is backward in his school work.

senses.definition: Of a culture, country, practice etc. undeveloped or unsophisticated.
senses.example: They were a backward people without any writing.

senses.definition: Slow to apprehend; having difficulties in learning.
senses.example: a backward child

senses.definition: Lacking progressive or enlightened thought; outdated.
senses.example: The party’s ideas and policies are very backward.

senses.definition: Late or behindhand.
senses.example: a backward season

senses.definition: Reluctant or unwilling to advance or act; shy.
senses.example: She certainly isn’t backward in coming forward!

senses.definition: Of a pawn, further behind than pawns of the same color on adjacent files and unable to be moved forward safely.
On that part of the field behind the batsman's popping crease.
Further behind the batsman's popping crease than something else.
At, near or towards the rear of something.
senses.example: The passenger turned around and walked backward, towards the tail of the aircraft.

senses.definition: In a direction opposite to that in which someone or something is facing or normally pointing.
senses.example: He tilted his head backward.

senses.definition: In a direction opposite to the usual direction of movement.
senses.example: In reverse gear the wheel turns backward.

senses.definition: Oppositely to the desired direction of progress, or from a better to a worse state.
senses.example: This project seems to be going backward.

senses.definition: In a reversed orientation; back to front.
senses.example: He had his cap on backward.

senses.definition: In a reversed order or sequence.
senses.example: A palindrome reads the same backward as forward.

senses.definition: Toward or into the past.
senses.example: As we begin the new millennium, it behoves us to look backward as well as forward.

senses.definition: By way of reflection; reflexively. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
The state behind or past.
(dated) To keep back, to delay, to retard.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Toward the back, or in the direction opposite to the one you are facing or moving.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Pronounce the 'w' clearly, as in 'BAK-wurd', and keep the final d; the second syllable is a reduced r-colored vowel, not a full 'ard'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'backward' for both adverb and adjective, and 'backwards' is also common as an adverb, especially in everyday speech. As an adjective, 'backward' is standard: say 'a backward step', not 'a backwards step'. Be careful when using 'backward' to describe a person, a community or a country, because it can mean underdeveloped or old-fashioned and may sound offensive.

distinctions.note: In American English the two are nearly interchangeable as adverbs, though 'backward' is more common in fixed phrases and as an adjective.
'Back' can be an adverb of location meaning 'to the place you came from,' while 'backward' describes the direction itself.
'Reverse' implies a complete undoing or a change of direction in a machine or process, while 'backward' describes simply moving toward the rear.

examples.everyday: Can you back the car up a little more? Just slowly backward so you don't hit the mailbox.
examples.professional: The new API is backward compatible, so existing clients will keep working without changes.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the reform movement looked backward to an idealized past rather than forward toward a new political order.

nuance.analogy: Like a car in reverse gear: the engine is running and the wheels are turning, but the direction is opposite to the way the car is facing.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English bakward, from back and -ward, meaning 'toward'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a backwards step' or 'backwards compatibility' in formal writing; American technical and formal writing prefers 'backward' before a noun.
Using 'backward' to describe a person or country in a neutral way, which can sound insulting.

senses.definition: Teasing.
Joking; jesting.
That teases.

core.definition: Teasing or joking playfully with someone; the present participle of 'banter'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'er' is a rhotic American 'r', not a separate 'uh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes friendly teasing that people enjoy, though it can sound negative if the teasing is cutting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bantering' to describe ongoing playful talk: 'They were bantering all through dinner.' It is conversational and common in everyday speech. A natural reply is 'Ha, they always do that.'

distinctions.note: 'Joking' is any humorous talk, while 'bantering' implies an ongoing back-and-forth exchange.
Arguing is serious disagreement. Bantering is playful and not meant to win a point.

examples.everyday: My neighbor and I were bantering about our lawns over the fence this morning.
examples.professional: The two engineers were bantering during the standup, but they stayed focused on the deadline.
examples.analytical: In this scene, the bantering characters reveal intimacy that their formal dialogue hides.

nuance.analogy: Like tossing a ball back and forth: the fun lies in the rhythm of the exchange.
nuance.etymology: From 'banter' plus the '-ing' suffix; the root origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'bantering' as a noun for a single joke; it usually describes an ongoing exchange.
Stressing the second syllable.

senses.definition: A lawyer with the right to speak and argue as an advocate in higher lawcourts.

core.definition: In Britain and Commonwealth countries, a lawyer who argues cases in higher courts; Americans would say trial lawyer or attorney.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ister is reduced to an r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'stur', not 'stir' or 'ster'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it is a British term, so in the US it can sound foreign or overly formal.
nuance.usage_note: This word is British, and Americans rarely use it because the US has no equivalent job title. In American courts, say attorney or trial lawyer. You might hear barrister in a British television show or in discussions of Commonwealth law.

distinctions.note: Attorney is the common American term for a lawyer who represents clients in court and in other legal matters.
In Britain, a solicitor handles legal advice and paperwork, while a barrister argues cases in court; the US has no such split.

examples.everyday: My friend from London is a barrister, and she's always in court.
examples.professional: Our legal team hired a London barrister for the cross-border dispute.
examples.analytical: The distinction between barrister and solicitor in English law reflects a historical division between advocacy and advice.

nuance.analogy: A barrister is like a courtroom specialist, the performer who argues the case in front of the judge.
nuance.etymology: From bar, the railing in a courtroom where advocates stood, plus -ister, a suffix for an agent.
common_mistakes: Confusing barrister with barista, the coffee-shop worker
Using barrister for an American lawyer; say attorney instead

senses.definition: The particular kind of ball used in the sport of basketball.
A sport in which two opposing teams of five players strive to put a ball through a hoop.
senses.example: to play basketball

senses.definition: To play basketball.
To throw in a similar way to when shooting a basketball.

core.definition: A team sport in which two teams of five players score points by shooting a ball through a raised hoop, or the ball used in that game.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BAS, and reduce the middle syllable to a quick kit. The final syllable is bawl with a clear l, and it is weaker than the first, so do not give all three syllables equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Basketball is a very popular American sport, especially in schools, colleges, and neighborhood parks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use basketball for both the sport and the ball, and hoops is a casual slang term for the game. Basketball games are a big social event in high schools and colleges, and March Madness is the popular name for the NCAA tournament. Saying basketball game or play basketball is completely natural.

distinctions.note: Volleyball players hit a ball over a net without a hoop, while basketball players shoot into a hoop and may run with the ball.
Hoops is informal American slang for basketball, so it is friendly in conversation but not formal.

examples.everyday: Do you want to play basketball at the park after work?
examples.professional: The sales team organized a basketball tournament as a team-building event this quarter.
examples.analytical: Basketball's emphasis on spacing and transition has changed how coaches think about efficiency.

nuance.analogy: Basketball is like a fast chess match on a court, where every possession changes the position of the whole board.
nuance.etymology: It combines basket and ball, and James Naismith invented the game in 1891, using peach baskets as goals.
common_mistakes: Writing basket ball as two words
Giving all three syllables equal stress

conversation.text: Do you want to shoot some hoops? I've got a basketball.
We watch college basketball every March.
He's tall, so everybody asks him if he plays basketball.

senses.definition: Of property (real estate): located on a beach.
The portion of land or property that runs alongside and facing a beach.

core.definition: Located on or directly facing a beach, usually used for valuable property such as homes, hotels or condos.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BEACH. The vowel in 'front' is short, like 'uh', not 'ahh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for real estate, because it suggests prestige and a great view. It can sound expensive or exclusive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beachfront mainly in real estate, travel and hotel listings. In casual talk, people often say 'right on the beach' instead, and 'oceanfront' is common when the view is of the ocean.

distinctions.note: Oceanfront means facing the ocean, while beachfront means facing a beach, which might be on a lake or bay.
Beachside is looser and means near the beach, while beachfront usually implies direct access or a view from the property.

examples.everyday: We stayed at a beachfront hotel, so we could walk to the sand in our pajamas.
examples.professional: The listing says beachfront, but the lot is actually across the road, so check the deed before you buy.
examples.analytical: Beachfront status carries social and economic meaning, as it marks property where access to water becomes a premium good.

nuance.analogy: Beachfront property is like a front-row seat for the ocean.
common_mistakes: Saying 'beach front' as two words in formal writing. Americans usually write it as one word.
Using it for any property near the sand. Beachfront means directly on or facing the beach.

conversation.text: They just bought a beachfront house, so we're all invited this summer.
Let's grab lunch at that beachfront bar with the outdoor deck.
Beachfront parking fills up by nine on weekends.

senses.definition: A person who believes; especially regarding religion.
senses.example: She's a believer in life after death.

core.definition: A person who has faith in God or a religion, or who firmly accepts something as true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: bih-LEEV. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, not a British 'uh' with no r.

nuance.connotation: Positive in religious settings, where it describes a committed person. Outside religion it can sound neutral or slightly ironic, as in 'a believer in conspiracy theories.'
nuance.usage_note: In American church life, 'believer' usually means a committed Christian, and people say 'fellow believers' or 'new believers.' Outside church, Americans say 'a believer in' something, such as 'a believer in second chances.' In casual talk, 'Christian' or 'a person of faith' is more common when you want to describe someone's religion.

distinctions.note: A disciple is a learner who follows a teacher closely, while a believer is defined by trust or faith in what is taught.
An unbeliever does not accept the belief in question, so the two words are opposites in religious use.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a believer, so she goes to church every Sunday and invites us to dinner afterward.
examples.professional: Our church's new-member class is for anyone who is a believer and wants to join the congregation.
examples.analytical: Paul uses the language of faith to describe believers as those who receive the gospel and are made right with God through trust.

nuance.etymology: From 'believe' (Old English belēfan) with the agent suffix '-er.'
common_mistakes: Using 'believer' for any person who merely has an opinion; in religious use it means someone with faith
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (BEE-liever) instead of the second
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek words behind 'believer' are pisteuō (to believe, to trust) and pistos (faithful, trusting). The RSV uses 'believe' for pisteuō and speaks of believers as those who trust God and Christ. John 3:16 says whoever believes in Jesus should not perish but have eternal life. Acts 2:44 describes all who believed living together and sharing their goods. Romans 1:16 says the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith.

senses.definition: The act of bequeathing or leaving by will.
The transfer of property upon the owner's death according to the will of the deceased.
That which is left by will; a legacy.
That which has been handed down or transmitted.
A person's inheritance; an amount of property given by will.
To give as a bequest; bequeath.

core.definition: Property or money that someone leaves to another person in a will, or the act of leaving it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The 'qu' is pronounced 'kw,' and the final 'st' is a clean cluster, not 'bih-KWEST-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually describes a gift of money or property, often with a sense of generosity or honor to the giver.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bequest' in estate planning, charity, and legal contexts, for example 'a bequest to the university.' In casual talk, people say 'inheritance' or 'left me something in his will.' Using 'bequest' for ordinary gifts sounds stiff.

distinctions.note: Inheritance is the general term for property received after death, whether by will or law. A bequest specifically means something given by will.
A legacy can be money, property, or a lasting influence on the world. A bequest is more narrowly a gift made in a will.

examples.everyday: My aunt left a bequest to the local library, and everyone in town was touched by it.
examples.professional: The foundation recorded a six-figure bequest from the estate, which will fund the new data science scholarship.
examples.analytical: A bequest is more than a transfer of wealth; it is a moral statement about what the dead person valued.

nuance.analogy: A bequest is like a sealed gift you leave on the table for someone, to be opened only after you are gone.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English bequeste, from bequethen, 'to bequeath.'
common_mistakes: Using 'bequest' for everyday gifts, which sounds overly formal.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Confusing it with 'request,' which is a different word.

bequest.etymology: From Middle English *biqueste*, *bequeste* (“will, testament, bequest”), from *be* + *queste*, from Old English **cwist*, **cwiss* (“saying”) (compare, *ġecwis*, *uncwisse*, etc.), from Proto-Germanic **kwissiz* (“saying”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: One who is narrow-mindedly devoted to their own ideas and groups, and intolerant of (people of) differing ideas, races, genders, religions, politics, etc.

core.definition: A person who stubbornly holds prejudiced views and refuses to tolerate people who think, believe, or look different.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BIG. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like uht, not like the long o in boat.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; calling someone a bigot is an accusation, so it is usually used only for clearly intolerant behavior or views.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bigot as a strong insult in political, religious, and social debates, so calling someone a bigot casually can start an argument. It usually refers to prejudice about race, religion, gender, or sexuality. To criticize a remark or belief, say it is bigoted rather than calling the person a bigot.

distinctions.note: Prejudiced describes a biased attitude that can be mild, while bigot describes a person whose intolerance is rigid and often hostile.
A zealot is passionately devoted to a cause, whereas a bigot is defined by intolerance toward people who differ.

examples.everyday: My uncle is stubborn, but I wouldn't call him a bigot; he just refuses to listen.
examples.professional: Calling a coworker a bigot in a team meeting would shut the discussion down, so keep feedback focused on specific behavior.
examples.analytical: A bigot's error is not only a false belief but a refusal to let evidence or other people's experience change that belief.

nuance.analogy: A bigot is like someone wearing tinted glasses who insists everything is that color and never takes them off.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Old French bigot, a term for a narrow-minded or overly pious person; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a long o, as in BIG-oht; it is a reduced schwa, BIG-uht.
Using bigot for anyone who simply disagrees with you; the word implies prejudice and intolerance, not just a different opinion.

bigot.etymology: From French *bigot* (“a sanctimonious person; a religious hypocrite”), from Middle French *bigot*, from Old French *bigot*, of disputed origin.

senses.definition: In a bland manner.

core.definition: In a calm, mild or unemotional way, often without showing much interest or feeling.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final -ly is pronounced as 'lee' with a long e, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests a lack of emotion or color, sometimes a deliberate hiding of feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blandly in writing and speech to describe someone who answers without emotion or who presents something without flair. For example, 'he blandly said no' suggests a flat, unexcited answer. In casual talk people might say 'with a straight face' or 'like it was nothing' instead.

distinctions.note: Calmly means peacefully and in control; blandly suggests a lack of feeling or interest, which can be negative.
Coolly suggests deliberate composure or aloofness; blandly suggests a flat, unremarkable manner.

examples.everyday: When I asked if he wanted pizza, he just shrugged and blandly said whatever.
examples.professional: The vendor blandly presented the same slide deck we had already rejected twice.
examples.analytical: The author blandly reports atrocities as routine events, which makes the reader feel their moral weight more sharply.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather report read in a monotone, with no feeling in the voice at all.
nuance.etymology: From bland, from Latin blandus, 'soft, smooth', plus the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ly as 'lie'; it is 'lee'.
Using blandly to mean kindly; the word suggests a lack of feeling, not warmth.

senses.definition: Agent noun of block (“obstruct or prevent”); something that blocks something else.
senses.example: an ad blocker

senses.definition: One who prevents another user from contacting them electronically.
An application or feature that stops or impedes something.
senses.example: an ad blocker

senses.definition: A bug or issue that prevents software from being released.
A gatekeeper who refuses the marketer access to the person they wish to contact.
A close-fitting rectangular glove worn by a goalie in multiple forms of hockey.
A blocker bet.
A playing card, needed by one player, that is held by another.
A person who roughly shapes a diamond.
A person who blocks (stretches or moulds) or more generally makes knitted items, hats, books (or book covers), shoes, etc.
A resident or member of a particular block.
Synonym of block ornament (“a cheap piece of meat of poor quality”).
One who blocks or impedes the movement of an opponent.
A defensive or low-scoring batter.

Any of various medications that block (inhibit) the activity of a chemical messenger or its receptors, such as cardiac conduction modifiers (e.g. alpha-blockers, beta-blockers), gastric acid inhibitors (H₂ histamine blockers), puberty blockers, and others.

core.definition: Something that stops or prevents something else, such as a medicine, a software tool, or an obstacle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, not a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use, such as 'ad blocker'. It can be negative when describing a person who obstructs progress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blocker in everyday tech talk, as in 'ad blocker' or 'pop-up blocker', and in medicine, as in 'beta blocker'. In meetings, it can describe someone who can stop a decision. In football, a blocker is a player who blocks for the ball carrier.

distinctions.note: A barrier is a physical object that keeps people or things out; a blocker can be a drug, app, or person that stops a process.
Obstacle is a general problem to overcome; blocker suggests something designed or used to stop an action.

examples.everyday: Turn on your ad blocker, these pages are full of pop-ups.
examples.professional: Our security team deployed a blocker that stops logins from unrecognized foreign addresses.
examples.analytical: The philosopher treats fear as a blocker of genuine inquiry, something that obstructs the mind's capacity to examine evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a bouncer at the door who keeps certain people out.
nuance.etymology: From block (verb) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -er as a full 'ah' sound; it should be a soft, reduced r-ending.
Confusing blocker, the thing or person that stops something, with blocking, the action itself.

conversation.text: Any blockers I can help with?
My main blocker is that I still don't have access to the database.
Let's raise that blocker in standup so someone can fix it.

senses.definition: A series of chisel points mounted on one piece of steel. For example, the toothed stone chisel shown here.
A broad chisel for stone-cutting.
A spit for cooking food.
An awl; a bodkin; also, a wooden rod or pin, sharpened at each end, used by thatchers.
A spit-like start on the head of a young stag.
The stick from which candle wicks are suspended for dipping.
The pin in a lock which enters the barrel of the key.
To make a hole in, especially a cask of liquor, and put in a tap in order to draw the liquid.
To open, to make an opening into; to pierce.
senses.example: French knights at Agincourt were unable to broach the English line.

senses.definition: To begin discussion about (something).
senses.example: I broached the subject of contraceptives carefully when the teenager mentioned his promiscuity.

senses.definition: To be turned sideways to oncoming waves, especially large or breaking waves.
senses.example: The small boat broached and nearly sank, because of the large waves.

senses.definition: To cause to turn sideways to oncoming waves, especially large or breaking waves (usually followed by to; also figurative).
senses.example: Each time we came around into the wind, the sea broached our bow.

senses.definition: To break the surface of the water.
senses.example: Diving officer, broach the ship!

core.definition: To bring up a difficult or sensitive subject for the first time, especially in conversation.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, so the stress is on the whole word. It rhymes with coach and approach, not with brooch, which has a long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It signals that the topic is sensitive or awkward to raise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use broach mostly in phrases like broach the subject or broach the topic, usually for awkward matters such as money, health, or a breakup. In casual speech people more often say bring up. A natural reply is Yeah, I've been wanting to bring that up too.

distinctions.note: Bring up is the everyday phrase for raising any topic; broach suggests the topic is delicate or awkward.
A brooch is a decorative pin for clothing, pronounced with a long oo; it is a different word despite the similar spelling.

collocations: broach the idea with my manager

examples.everyday: I finally broached the subject of moving in together, and she said she was glad I brought it up.
examples.professional: I'd like to broach the timeline with the product team before we commit to the launch date.
examples.analytical: The essay broaches the problem of evil without offering a final answer, which makes its argument more honest.

nuance.analogy: Like cutting into a sealed jar: you open the topic that no one wanted to touch.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English broche, from Old French broche, meaning spike or spit; the sense of piercing came first and the figurative sense followed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like brooch with a long oo, as BROOCH; the vowel is the oh of coach.
Using broach to mean a jewelry pin, which confuses it with brooch.

broach.etymology: From Middle English *broche*, from Old French *broche*, from Vulgar Latin **brocca*, originally a feminine form of Latin *broccus*, perhaps ultimately of origin.

senses.definition: Cheap and showy; meretricious.

core.definition: Cheap, flashy, and showy, but of poor quality, like imitation goods made to look more valuable than they are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BRUM, and make the ending a quiet 'juhm'. Do not pronounce it as 'brum-AH-jem'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes things that look valuable but are cheap or fake.
nuance.usage_note: Brummagem is mainly British and literary, and Americans almost never use it. Americans would say cheap, tacky, gaudy, or knockoff to describe the same idea. Lowercase brummagem is the adjective, while capitalized Brummagem refers to Birmingham, England.

distinctions.note: Tawdry is showy and cheap in a more morally judgmental way, often about appearance or taste.
Flashy only means attention-getting, while brummagem adds the sense that the thing is cheap or fake.
Kitschy describes things deliberately campy or retro, while brummagem is always a criticism of poor quality.

examples.everyday: That chandelier in the lobby looks fancy, but it's pure cheap brummagem, so don't pay much for it.
examples.professional: The vendor's sample looked premium, but the brummagem finish would chip after a month of normal use.
examples.analytical: The institution's prestige rested on glossy branding and brummagem rhetoric rather than on sustained substance.

nuance.analogy: Brummagem goods are like a stage prop that looks like a real castle from the audience but is made of painted cardboard.
nuance.etymology: From Brummagem, an old name for Birmingham, England, a city long associated with cheap, showy metal goods.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing it when used as an adjective, as in 'brummagem jewelry' rather than 'Brummagem jewelry'.
Using it as a neutral description of Birmingham residents, which is outdated and confusing.

brummagem.etymology: From Birmingham, England where cheap manufactured goods used to be produced.

senses.definition: Having buoyancy; able to float.
Lighthearted and lively.
senses.example: I’m in a buoyant mood.

senses.definition: Involving or engaged in much successful trade or activity.

core.definition: Able to float, or cheerful and lively, or describing a market or economy that is strong and active.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOY, which rhymes with 'toy'. The final -ant is weak and sounds like 'unt', so the word has two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests lightness, energy, and optimism, and is common in business news about markets and sales.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'in buoyant spirits' or 'a buoyant mood' in everyday speech, and 'a buoyant market' in business. It is neutral and polite, so it works well in both casual conversation and professional writing. Avoid it for a person who is just loud; use 'upbeat' or 'cheerful' for that.

distinctions.note: Upbeat is informal and describes a positive attitude in conversation. Buoyant suggests a lifted, energetic quality and works for markets too.
Cheerful describes a happy disposition. Buoyant suggests a lively lift in spirit or activity that can be sustained over time.
Bouncy describes physical bounce or a playful, springy manner. Buoyant is more formal and can describe economies or markets.

examples.everyday: She's in a buoyant mood since she got the new job.
examples.professional: Demand has been buoyant all year, so we're raising the sales target for next quarter.
examples.analytical: The buoyant claims of the early essay give way to more cautious reasoning in the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a beach ball bobbing on the surface of a pool.
nuance.etymology: From buoy plus the adjective suffix -ant.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'BOO-yant' instead of 'BOY-unt'
Confusing it with 'bouncy', which describes springy movement rather than a lifted spirit

senses.definition: In a calm manner; coolly.

core.definition: In a peaceful, controlled way, without showing anger, panic, or strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The l is silent, so the word sounds like 'KAHM-lee,' not 'KAHLM-lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes composure, especially under pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calmly in everyday speech and at work, especially when describing how someone handled a situation, such as 'He calmly explained the rules.' It is a natural, neutral word and does not sound formal. A common reply to someone describing a calm reaction is 'That's really good, you kept your cool.'

distinctions.note: Quietly describes low volume or a lack of noise, while calmly describes a composed emotional manner.
Patiently implies waiting and tolerance over time, while calmly describes a steady, composed manner in the moment.

examples.everyday: The waiter calmly said the kitchen was running late and brought us bread while we waited.
examples.professional: During the incident call, she calmly walked the team through each step of the failover.
examples.analytical: The speaker calmly distinguishes between genuine doubt and mere rhetorical provocation, which makes her argument persuasive.

nuance.analogy: Speaking calmly is like walking across ice slowly and steadily rather than running and slipping.
nuance.etymology: From calm plus the adverbial suffix -ly; calm comes from Old French calme, from Medieval Latin cauma.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the l in calmly.
Using calmly to mean quietly when you mean that the room was not noisy.

senses.definition: In writing or editing, to write (something: either an entire word or text, or just the initial letter(s) thereof) in capital letters, in upper case.
senses.example: In German, all nouns are capitalized.

senses.definition: To contribute or acquire capital (money or other resources) for.
senses.example: Some states require proof that a new venture is properly capitalized before the state will issue a certificate of incorporation.

senses.definition: To convert into capital, i.e. to get cash or similar immediately fungible resources for some less fungible property or source of future income.
senses.example: If we obtain a loan using the business as collateral, the effect will be to capitalize our next ten years of income, giving us cash today that we can use to buy out our competitor.

senses.definition: To treat as capital, not as an expense.
To profit or to obtain an advantage.
senses.example: The home team took several shots on goal but was unable to capitalize until late in the game.

senses.definition: To seize, as an opportunity; to obtain a benefit from; to invest on something profitable.
senses.example: The home team appeared to have the advantage throughout the game, and finally capitalized on their opponents' weakness with just two minutes remaining, scoring several points in quick succession.

core.definition: To take advantage of an opportunity (usually with 'on'); also, to write a word or letter in capital letters.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on KAP, and the -ize ending sounds like 'eyes'. The middle t is a quick flap that sounds almost like a d, so it is not a hard t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Capitalize on an opportunity usually sounds smart and strategic, though it can sound exploitative when used about people's weaknesses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'capitalize on' in business, sports, and everyday talk, as in 'we should capitalize on the good press.' Use it with an opportunity or trend, not a person. The writing sense appears in style guides and in spellcheck, as in 'capitalize the first letter.'

distinctions.note: Exploit usually implies unfair use of someone; capitalize on is neutral or positive about using an opportunity.
Take advantage of is a close everyday synonym; capitalize on sounds more businesslike.

collocations: capitalize every word in the title

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is capitalizing on the summer crowds by renting out her garage for parking.
examples.professional: We should capitalize on the momentum from the launch by sending the follow-up email this week.
examples.analytical: Marx argues that the system lets owners capitalize on labor, turning human effort into surplus value.

nuance.analogy: Capitalizing on an opportunity is like catching a wave at the right moment; if you wait too long, it passes.
nuance.etymology: From capital, from Latin capitalis, of the head; the writing sense comes from capital letters.
common_mistakes: Saying 'capitalize from' or 'capitalize of'; the correct preposition is on.
Spelling it 'capitolize' with an o; the spelling is capitalize with an a.

capitalize.etymology: From *capital* + *ize*, the first element ultimately from Latin *capitālis* (“of the head”).

senses.definition: Of fundamental importance; crucial, pivotal.
senses.example: a cardinal rule

senses.definition: Used to describe quantity (e.g. zero, one, two, three), as opposed to an ordinal number indicating relative position. (See Cardinal_number.)
Having a bright red color (from the color of a Catholic cardinal’s cassock).
Being one of the signs Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn, associated with initiation, creation, and force.
Of or relating to the cardinal directions (north, south, east and west).
senses.example: a cardinal mark

senses.definition: One of the officials appointed by the pope in the Roman Catholic Church, ranking only below the pope, equal to the patriarchs, constituting the special college which elects the pope.
