Any of various species of New-World passerine songbird in the genus Cardinalis, or in the family Cardinalidae more generally, or of similar appearance and once considered to be related to the former; so called because of their red plumage. (See Wikipedia article for taxonomical information.)
A deep red color, somewhat less vivid than scarlet, the traditional color of a Catholic cardinal's cassock.
senses.example: cardinal:

senses.definition: Ellipsis of cardinal number, a number indicating quantity, or the size of a set (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3). (See Cardinal_number.)
Ellipsis of cardinal numeral, a word used to represent a cardinal number.
Ellipsis of cardinal flower (Lobelia cardinalis), a flowering plant.
Ellipsis of cardinal tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi), a freshwater fish.
A woman's short cloak with a hood, originally made of scarlet cloth.
A fairy chess piece which combines the moves of the bishop and the knight.

core.definition: One of the senior Roman Catholic clergy appointed by the pope, ranking just below him and forming the college that elects new popes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is often dropped, so say KAHRD-nuhl rather than kar-di-NAL. Keep the r clear, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a church title; it carries prestige and formality, while as a bird or color name it is cheerful and warm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cardinal for the church official mainly in news, religious, and Catholic contexts, and address one as 'Your Eminence.' In everyday talk, 'cardinal' most often means the red songbird or the bright red color, so context matters. Bishops are not cardinals unless the pope appoints them to that rank.

distinctions.note: A bishop governs a diocese, while a cardinal is a special rank, usually held by a bishop or archbishop, that carries a role in electing the pope.
The pope is the head of the Roman Catholic Church, and cardinals rank just below him and advise him and elect his successor.

examples.everyday: My aunt in Boston says she once sat next to a cardinal at a wedding, and she still talks about it.
examples.professional: Our diocese's communications office sent out the press release about the cardinal's visit to the cathedral.
examples.analytical: The cardinals gathered in conclave form a college that shares in the pope's governance of the universal Church.

nuance.analogy: A cardinal is like a senior partner who has the right to choose the firm's next CEO.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cardinalis, principal or chief, from cardo, hinge, so something on which other things turn.
common_mistakes: Calling any senior priest or bishop a cardinal, when the title is specifically given by the pope.
Assuming the bird and the church official share a stress pattern or pronunciation; the bird is also KAHR-dn-ul, but usage differs in context.

cardinal.etymology: From Middle French *cardinal*, from Latin *cardinālis* (“pertaining to a hinge, hence applied to that on which something turns or depends, important, principal, chief”), from cardin, *cardō* (“hinge”) + *-ālis*, adjectival suffix.

senses.definition: Synonym of catastrophic interference.

core.definition: In machine learning, a sudden, severe loss of previously learned abilities when a neural network is trained on new data.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'strah' in 'catastrophic' and on 'get' in 'forgetting'. The 'r' in 'forgetting' is rhotic, and in General American 'strah' has the same vowel as 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious failure mode in AI systems, and engineers use it as a problem to be solved.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in machine learning research, AI engineering, and technical discussions of continual learning. It is precise jargon, so use it with colleagues who work in the field. Outside that setting, say the model 'forgot what it learned' or 'lost its earlier skills'.

distinctions.note: The two terms are generally treated as synonyms in the literature. Catastrophic forgetting is more common in recent papers, while interference emphasizes the cause as competing updates.
Overfitting means a model learns the training data too closely and fails to generalize to new data. Catastrophic forgetting happens when training on a new task erases performance on an old one.

examples.everyday: My friend who works on robots says the model kept learning new tricks but kind of forgot the old ones, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.
examples.professional: After we fine-tuned the language model on the new support tickets, its accuracy on the billing questions dropped, so we need a fix for catastrophic forgetting.
examples.analytical: Catastrophic forgetting exposes a deep tension between plasticity, the ability to learn new things, and stability, the ability to keep old knowledge.

nuance.analogy: It is like a student who studies chemistry so hard that they completely forget the algebra they learned last semester.
nuance.etymology: Catastrophic comes from Greek katastrophē, 'overturning'. Forgetting comes from Old English forgietan. The term was popularized in connectionist research in the late 1980s.
common_mistakes: Using catastrophic forgetting for gradual forgetting, when the term means sudden and severe loss.
Stressing the wrong syllable in 'catastrophic', such as 'kuh-TAS-truh-fik'.

conversation.text: Catastrophic forgetting happens when training on a new task wipes out performance on earlier tasks.
After fine-tuning on legal documents, the model showed catastrophic forgetting on general questions.
Mixing in some original training data is a simple way to reduce catastrophic forgetting.

senses.definition: Something that is generated within itself, or assigns itself a purpose.

core.definition: Something that causes or grounds its own existence, or gives itself its own purpose or reason; self-caused.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are Latin, and the stress falls on the first syllable of each, so say KAW-zuh and SOO-ee. Do not pronounce 'sui' as 'swee' or 'sweet.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in philosophy, and it can be used to critique or defend an idea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use causa sui almost only in philosophy, theology and academic writing, usually in discussions of God, the self or the ground of being. Some writers italicize it. In casual speech, people say 'self-caused' or 'self-grounding' instead.

distinctions.note: Self-caused is the English gloss and is usable in ordinary writing; causa sui is a technical Latin phrase common in philosophy and theology.
Sui generis means unique in its kind; causa sui means generated by or grounding itself, so the two are not interchangeable.

collocations: reject the idea of causa sui

examples.everyday: My philosophy friend joked that the universe could not be causa sui, so somebody had to start it.
examples.professional: In our ethics seminar, the speaker argued that a self-directed agent is not causa sui, since its values come from upbringing and culture.
examples.analytical: Spinoza's God is causa sui in the sense that its essence involves existence, so nothing outside it is needed to explain its being.

nuance.analogy: A self-sustaining fire that keeps itself burning from its own heat, with no outside match.
nuance.etymology: Latin, literally 'cause of itself,' from causa (cause) and sui (of itself).
common_mistakes: Using causa sui for a self-made person in everyday speech, which sounds odd; it is a technical metaphysical term.
Pronouncing sui as 'swee' rather than 'SOO-ee.'

senses.definition: Synonym of pure and virtuous, particularly.
senses.example: Theirs was a chaste marriage, loving and content.

senses.definition: Sexually pure, abstaining from immoral or unlawful sexual intercourse.
senses.example: Theirs was a chaste marriage, loving and content.

senses.definition: Synonym of celibate, abstaining from any sexual intercourse.
senses.example: Theirs was a chaste marriage, cold and sexless.

senses.definition: Synonym of virginal, innocent, having or providing no sexual knowledge or experience.
senses.example: Her upbringing had been so chaste that her first experience French kissing ended in a panicked dash to the Piggly Wiggly to buy a home pregnancy test, just in case.

senses.definition: Synonym of modest, particularly in reference to behavior expected of sexually pure women.
senses.example: I ask again what reason could a chaste woman possibly have for being out so late? and in that part of town? Your Honor, we repeat our motion that you recuse yourself from this case.

senses.definition: Synonym of austere, plain, unextravagant, particularly demure, sexually discreet.
senses.example: The chaste style of most early modern novels is elegant but intensely boring, particularly for teenagers too inexperienced to effectively read between the lines.

core.definition: Abstaining from sexual activity outside marriage, or from all sex, according to moral or religious standards; sexually pure.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with 'taste' and 'waste'. The final st is a clean consonant cluster, so do not add a vowel after the t.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting virtue and self-control. It can sound prim or old-fashioned, and it is often used neutrally to describe content, as in a chaste romance or family-friendly entertainment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chaste mainly in religious, literary or formal contexts, or to describe a romance that avoids physical intimacy. Calling a person chaste in ordinary conversation can sound stiff or like a judgment about their private life, so in everyday talk people say 'waiting until marriage' or 'not sexually active' instead. In writing, 'a chaste kiss' means a brief, nonsexual kiss.

distinctions.note: Pure is broader and can mean clean, unmixed or innocent; chaste refers specifically to sexual purity or abstinence.
Celibate means not marrying or having sex, usually by a deliberate vow; chaste describes sexual conduct and can apply to married people too.

examples.everyday: The old movie was so chaste that the couple only held hands and kissed on the cheek.
examples.professional: Keep the romance chaste in the script so it fits the network's family audience.
examples.analytical: Medieval courtly love often idealized a chaste devotion that was more about the lover's discipline than about physical desire.

nuance.analogy: Like a sealed jar kept shut on purpose, guarded by the owner's own choice.
nuance.etymology: From Old French chaste, from Latin castus, meaning pure or morally clean.
common_mistakes: Confusing chaste with chased, which is pronounced the same way but means pursued.
Adding a syllable and saying 'chay-stee' instead of one syllable.

chaste.etymology: From Middle English *chaste*, from Old French *chaste* (“morally pure”), from Latin *castus* (“pure”).

senses.definition: A device for measuring time, particularly a precision mechanism for measuring time of day.
senses.example: A wristwatch costs $20; a chronometer costs $20,000.

core.definition: A very accurate clock or watch, used especially to measure time precisely at sea or in science.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAH. The ch sounds like k, and the final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'tuhr'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It suggests precision and craftsmanship, and it is rarely used in casual conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chronometer mainly in maritime navigation, aviation, horology, and science. Most people say 'watch' or 'clock' in daily life, and calling an ordinary watch a chronometer would sound odd or overly technical. Enthusiasts may use it for high-precision watches with certification.

distinctions.note: A clock is any device that shows time, while a chronometer is a highly accurate instrument built for precise timekeeping.
A chronograph is a watch function that measures elapsed time, while a chronometer keeps accurate time of day.

examples.everyday: My dad calls his watch a chronometer, but it's really just a nice mechanical watch.
examples.professional: The lab calibrates each atomic chronometer against a national time standard every quarter.
examples.analytical: Harrison's marine chronometer solved the longitude problem by keeping accurate time while the ship was moving.

nuance.analogy: A chronometer is to an ordinary clock what a surgeon's scalpel is to a kitchen knife: built for precision.
nuance.etymology: From Greek chronos (time) and metron (measure).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as 'sh', as in 'shruh-NAH-mih-tuhr'. It is a k sound.
Confusing chronometer with chronograph. A chronograph measures intervals, while a chronometer keeps accurate time.

chronometer.etymology: From *chrono-* + *-meter*, possibly after the model of earlier French *chronomètre* (“metronome”), ultimately from Ancient Greek *χρόνος* (“time”) + *μέτρον* (“meter, measuring device”).

senses.definition: A small, exclusive group of individuals, usually having some common characteristic such as lifestyle or social status, or common purpose; specifically one formed for disreputable purposes, or which purports to be an authority on a particular matter; a cabal.
senses.example: This school used to be really friendly, but now everyone keeps to their own cliques.

senses.definition: A subgraph isomorphic to a complete graph.
senses.example: The problem of finding the largest clique in an arbitrary graph is NP-complete.

senses.definition: A group of related websites that link to each other, like a webring but with exclusive membership determined by the clique owner.

(historical) An informal faction in the Republic of China (1912–1949) led by one or more warlords exercising regional control through local armed forces (particularly during the Warlord Era); a regional junta.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Often followed by together.
To form a clique (“small, exclusive group of individuals, usually having some common characteristic”; noun sense 1); to associate with others in a clannish way.
To act with others secretly to gain a desired end; to plot, to scheme.

core.definition: A small, exclusive group of people who share interests or status and often shut others out. In graph theory, it is a set of points where every point connects to every other.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long ee sound and a hard k at the end. Do not use the French pronunciation klee-KAY, which sounds foreign in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative or mildly negative, because a clique implies exclusivity that leaves others out. The word is neutral when used in technical contexts like mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clique most often for high school or workplace groups that seem closed to newcomers, as in 'She's in the popular clique.' Saying 'They're a clique' about a friend group can sound judgmental, so use it carefully. A friendly reply is 'Yeah, they keep to themselves, but they're nice once you know them.'

distinctions.note: Group is neutral and can be any collection of people, while clique always suggests exclusivity and a closed circle.
Circle usually sounds warmer and more personal, as in 'my circle of friends,' while clique sounds more critical.
Faction is formal and usually refers to a political or organizational split, while clique refers to a social group.

examples.everyday: Mia's really nice, but her friends are a total clique, so it's hard to join in.
examples.professional: The senior engineers formed a clique on the chat channel, so new hires rarely got answers.
examples.analytical: Institutions that reward loyalty over merit tend to produce a clique that protects its members and excludes outsiders.

nuance.analogy: A cafeteria table that everyone knows is reserved for a small group, even though no sign says so.
nuance.etymology: From French clique, a set or gang, probably related to cliquer, to click or make a noise.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a French accent as klee-KAY, which is not standard American pronunciation.
Using clique for any group of friends in a neutral way, when the word usually implies exclusivity.

clique.etymology: The is borrowed from French *clique* (“exclusive group of individuals; group of people hired to applaud or boo, claque”), from *cliquer* (“to clap; to clack, to click”), ultimately of origin.

senses.definition: An abstraction that represents a function within an environment, a context consisting of the variables that are both bound at a particular time during the execution of the program and that are within the function's scope.
An event or occurrence that signifies an ending.
A feeling of completeness; the experience of an emotional conclusion, usually to a difficult period.
senses.example: to find emotional closure

senses.definition: A device to facilitate temporary and repeatable opening and closing.
The smallest set that both includes a given subset and possesses some given property.
The smallest closed set which contains the given set.
The act of shutting; a closing.
senses.example: the closure of a door, or of a chink

senses.definition: The act of shutting or closing something permanently or temporarily.
senses.example: The closure of Hammersmith Bridge means road traffic has to use Chiswick and Putney Bridges instead.

senses.definition: That which closes or shuts; that by which separate parts are fastened or closed.
A method of ending a parliamentary debate and securing an immediate vote upon a measure before a legislative body.
The phenomenon by which a group maintains its resources by the exclusion of others based on various criteria.
The process whereby the reader of a comic book infers the sequence of events by looking at the picture panels.
The element of packaging that closes a container.
The phenomenon whereby incomplete objects, shapes, and figures are perceived as complete.
To end the parliamentary debate on (an issue) by closure.

core.definition: A function bundled with references to the variables from the scope where it was created, so it can use them later.

pronunciation.tip: The -sure ending is pronounced like the s in measure, a zh sound, not like an s. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in programming. In everyday talk, the emotional sense of closure is positive, meaning relief at finally resolving something painful.
nuance.usage_note: Programmers use closure in Python, JavaScript, Kotlin, and other languages when discussing functions that capture variables. In conversation, Americans also say 'I need closure' to mean emotional resolution after a loss or breakup. Software teams often say lambda or anonymous function when they mean the syntax rather than the captured state.

distinctions.note: A lambda is a syntax for writing an anonymous function, while a closure is the function plus its captured environment, which a lambda often creates.
A callback is a function passed to another function to run later, and it is often a closure, but not every callback captures variables.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the bug happens because a closure is holding onto an old variable.
examples.professional: In the code review, I flagged the closure because it keeps a reference to the entire dataframe.
examples.analytical: A closure binds free variables to their defining environment, so the function's behavior depends on state that outlives its enclosing call.

nuance.analogy: A closure is like a backpack a function carries, packed with the variables from the place where it was born.
nuance.etymology: Closure comes from Middle English and Old French clore, from Latin claudere meaning to shut; the programming sense extends the general meaning of closing over an environment.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -sure ending as an s sound, like KLOH-sur, instead of the zh sound.
Using closure to mean closing a window or file; in programming it refers only to a function with captured variables.

closure.etymology: From Middle English *closure*, from Old French *closure*, from Late Latin *clausura*, from Latin *claudere* (“to close”); see and close.

senses.definition: The property of being coincident, occurring at the same time or place.
The appearance of a meaningful connection between events when there is none.
senses.example: That the two writers were born and died on the same day is just a coincidence, although there are many conspiracy theories about it.

senses.definition: A coincidence point.
A fixed point of a correspondence; a point of a variety corresponding to itself under a correspondence.

core.definition: An event or circumstance that happens by chance at the same time as another, seeming connected but not planned.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, IN, and the final syllable is reduced to a weak uh sound. Many learners say the middle as see-dens, but the vowel in the third syllable is a short i, so keep it quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound playful or mysterious depending on context, such as a striking chance meeting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say what a coincidence when they discover a shared link, like meeting someone from the same hometown. The phrase by coincidence is common in storytelling and news. A coincidence is not the same as a plan, so using it for intentional events sounds wrong.

distinctions.note: Chance means randomness in general, while coincidence stresses a noticeable match between two events that seems meaningful.
An accident is an unintended event that often causes harm, while a coincidence is a harmless matching of timing or circumstances.

examples.everyday: What a coincidence, my sister lives on the same street as you!
examples.professional: We found it was pure coincidence that both teams launched the same feature on the same day.
examples.analytical: A genuine causal link is different from a mere coincidence, and the study had to rule out the latter before making any claim.

nuance.analogy: A coincidence is like two songs on different playlists starting on the exact same beat by accident.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin coincidentia, from coincidere 'to fall together,' from co- 'together' plus incidere 'to fall upon.'
common_mistakes: Using coincident as a noun instead of coincidence.
Saying by coincident instead of by coincidence.

senses.definition: A polite formula used when one has not heard or understood what has been said, or to indicate surprise.
Used as a polite farewell to a visitor, inviting a return visit.

core.definition: Please repeat that; I did not catch or understand what you just said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GEN, which rhymes with 'den'. The second syllable of again is a reduced 'uh', so the phrase sounds like 'kum-uh-GEN' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when friendly; it can sound rude or challenging with a sharp tone or a stressed COME AGAIN?
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Come again?' in casual speech when they miss something, often on the phone. With a rising, friendly tone it is fine, but with a flat or sharp tone it can sound skeptical or confrontational. At work, use 'Sorry, could you repeat that?' or 'Sorry, I missed that.' The farewell sense, inviting someone to return, is old-fashioned and rarely used today.

distinctions.note: Excuse me? is polite in most settings, but stressed heavily it can express offense; come again is more casual.
Sorry, what? sounds informal and slightly dismissive in business settings; prefer 'Sorry, could you repeat that?' at work.

collocations: come again with the last part

examples.everyday: Come again? I missed the part about what time we're meeting.
examples.professional: Come again on the deadline? I thought we agreed on Thursday.
examples.analytical: When the speaker said come again, the listener was requesting a repetition, not contesting the claim.

nuance.analogy: It's like asking someone to rewind a recording because the sound cut out.
common_mistakes: Using come again in a formal email or to a manager, where it can sound abrupt.
Thinking it means please come back; the farewell sense is old and uncommon, so do not use it for the repeat meaning.

conversation.text: "The meeting's at six a.m." "Come again? Six in the morning?"
Come again? I didn't catch that.
"Your total is two hundred dollars." "Come again?"

senses.definition: The state or characteristic of being complementary.
A semantic relationship between two words wherein negative use of one entails the affirmative of the other with no gradability; the relation of binary antonyms.
The idea that physical phenomena may have (mutually contradictory) properties that cannot be observed simultaneously (e.g. wave-particle duality).

core.definition: The state of two things making up a whole when combined, or, in physics, the idea that some properties cannot be observed at the same time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAIR, the third syllable from the start. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the final -ity is 'ih-tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It describes a relationship without judgment, though in physics it carries the sense of an unavoidable tradeoff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use complementarity in technical writing, academic discussion, and science or philosophy classes. In everyday talk they would say 'how well things fit together' instead. The physics sense refers to the Copenhagen interpretation, so use it precisely in that context.

distinctions.note: A complement is a thing that completes another. Complementarity is the abstract relationship or principle of being complementary.
Compatibility means two things can work together without conflict. Complementarity means they fill each other's gaps to form a whole.

examples.everyday: Their skills have a nice complementarity, since she is organized and he is great with people.
examples.professional: The team's complementarity of backgrounds made the project stronger than any single hire could have.
examples.analytical: Bohr's principle of complementarity holds that wave and particle descriptions are mutually exclusive yet both necessary for a full account.

nuance.analogy: Like two sides of a coin, where you can see one face only by hiding the other.
nuance.etymology: From complementary plus -ity, the quality of being complementary; the physics sense was coined by Niels Bohr.
common_mistakes: Using it for complement, the thing itself, instead of the relationship.
Confusing the physics sense with a general idea of combination.

senses.definition: Performed through a concert of effort; done by agreement or in combination.
Having separate parts for voices and instruments.

core.definition: Done through coordinated planning and joint effort by several people or groups working together toward a common goal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SUR, and the first syllable reduces to 'kun'. The final -ed is pronounced 'id' after a t, so don't drop it or stress the noun form KAHN-surt.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests determination and organized effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concerted effort constantly in news, workplace emails, and public statements, usually to describe a strong and coordinated push. The phrase sounds more formal than everyday talk, where people might say a real push or everyone working together. You will hear it in offices, government reports, and community meetings. It works best when several people or groups are involved.

distinctions.note: Coordinated emphasizes that parts are arranged or timed well, while concerted emphasizes shared intent and effort among the people involved.
Joint means shared by two or more parties, often in a formal arrangement, while concerted emphasizes that the parties are acting together in a deliberate way.

examples.everyday: The neighbors made a concerted effort to clean up the park last weekend.
examples.professional: The team made a concerted push to clear the backlog before the release freeze.
examples.analytical: Tocqueville argued that American associations let citizens achieve through concerted action what they could never accomplish alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a choir singing one melody together, rather than each singer following a separate tune.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of concert, from Latin concertare 'to contend or strive together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing concerted with concerned, which means worried or involved and changes the meaning completely
Stressing the first syllable as KUN-sert, which follows the noun pattern rather than the adjective

senses.definition: In the nature of a conjecture, or based on a conjecture.
Something that is conjectural; a conjecture.

core.definition: Based on conjecture or guesswork rather than firm evidence; speculative and not proven.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'JEK'. The middle '-tur-' syllable is reduced to a quick 'chuh', so don't say the full 'tyoor' or 'choor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It signals that the claim lacks solid support, which can be useful for careful academic hedging or a mild criticism.
nuance.usage_note: You'll see this word mostly in academic writing, history, archaeology, and scientific reports, as in 'conjectural reconstruction'. In conversation, Americans usually say 'speculative' or 'just a guess'. Using 'conjectural' in casual talk can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: 'Speculative' often refers to ideas or investments with high risk. 'Conjectural' stresses that the claim is not supported by enough evidence.
'Hypothetical' describes an assumed case for discussion. 'Conjectural' describes a claim someone is actually proposing as possibly true.

examples.everyday: Nobody knows why the old barn was built that way, so any story about it is pretty conjectural.
examples.professional: Those churn numbers are conjectural until we get the actual cancellation data from billing.
examples.analytical: Much of early Christian history rests on conjectural reconstructions, since the surviving sources are fragmentary.

nuance.analogy: A conjectural claim is like a map with the coastline sketched in pencil: it shows where the land probably is, but nobody has surveyed it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjectura, from conicere, 'to throw together, infer', from com- and jacere, 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KON-jek-chur-ul) instead of the second.
Using 'conjectural' as a verb or noun; the noun is 'conjecture' and the adjective is 'conjectural'.

senses.definition: To cause consternation in; to dismay.

core.definition: To fill someone with alarm, dismay or confusion, often to the point that they cannot think or act clearly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KON. The middle syllable -ster- is reduced, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes strong alarm or dismay, usually caused by something sudden or shocking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use consternate in conversation. It appears mostly in writing, news and literary description, and is usually passive: 'the board was consternated by the news.' In speech, people say shocked, alarmed or freaked out.

distinctions.note: Alarm is a general word for fear or worry about danger; consternate suggests bewildered dismay, often caused by something unexpected.
Dismay is milder and more personal; consternate implies a more disruptive and confusing shock.

examples.professional: The sudden delay in the data pipeline consternated the product team, so we scheduled an emergency call.
examples.analytical: Hume's skeptical arguments consternated many readers who expected reason to settle the question of causation.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden alarm in a quiet office, leaving everyone frozen and looking at one another.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consternare, 'to throw into confusion or dismay', the root of consternation.
common_mistakes: Using consternate for mild surprise, when it means strong alarm and confusion.
Saying the verb with the noun's stress pattern, as in kahn-ster-NAYT, instead of KAHN-stur-nayt.

senses.definition: To use up.
senses.example: The power plant consumes 30 tons of coal per hour.

senses.definition: To eat.
senses.example: Baby birds consume their own weight in food each day.

senses.definition: To completely occupy the thoughts or attention of.
senses.example: Desire consumed him.

senses.definition: To destroy completely.
senses.example: The building was consumed by fire.

senses.definition: To obtain and use goods or services as an individual.
senses.example: In a materialistic society, individuals are taught to consume, consume, consume.

senses.definition: To absorb information, especially through the mass media.
senses.example: The Internet has changed the way we consume news.

core.definition: To eat or drink something, or to use something up completely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable with a long oo sound, like soom. The first syllable is a weak uh sound, so it sounds like kun, not kon.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; 'consumed by' is often negative, suggesting being overwhelmed.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people say 'eat,' 'drink' or 'use up,' and consume sounds formal or technical. It is common in writing about energy, food and the economy, as in 'the car consumes less gas.' 'Consumed by' means completely absorbed and is used in casual and formal speech alike, often with a negative tone.

distinctions.note: Eat is everyday and casual; consume is formal or technical and can mean using up anything, not only food.
Use is neutral and general; consume implies that something is used up or gone.
Absorb suggests taking something in, often positively; consume often means taking over completely, sometimes negatively.

examples.everyday: We try not to consume too much sugar, so we skip soda at dinner.
examples.professional: The new service will consume less memory, which should lower our cloud costs.
examples.analytical: Modern media does not merely inform people; it consumes their attention and turns every moment into a product to be sold.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that consumes wood, using up what it burns until nothing is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consumere, to use up, from con- (completely) and sumere, to take up.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I consumed a sandwich' in casual talk; 'ate' is more natural.
Misspelling it as 'consumtion' or confusing it with 'consumer' in writing.
Using 'consumed in' instead of 'consumed by' or 'consumed with.'

consume.etymology: From Middle English *consumen*, from Old French *consumer*, from Latin *consumo*, from *con-* + *sūmō*, from *sub* + *emō*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **h₁em-* (“to take, distribute”), possibly related to the root **nem-* (“to take or give one's…

senses.definition: Secret, surreptitious, concealed.
senses.example: covert operations

senses.definition: (rare) Hidden, covered over; overgrown, sheltered.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) Under coverture.
senses.example: feme covert
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: A covering.
A disguise.
A hiding place.
Area of thick undergrowth where animals hide.
A feather that covers the bases of flight feathers.

core.definition: Done or kept secret, especially to avoid being seen or noticed by others. Often used for planned actions that are hidden on purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a short, r-colored 'ert' with no 't' sound released. Do not confuse it with 'covet,' which has a different vowel and stress pattern in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is neutral when describing official secret operations, but it suggests deception or wrongdoing when describing private behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'covert' most often for government, military, police, or corporate activities that are deliberately hidden, such as covert surveillance or covert operations. In everyday talk, 'secret' or 'undercover' is more natural. Calling someone's glance 'covert' sounds slightly formal and dramatic.

distinctions.note: Overt means open and visible, the direct opposite of covert.
Clandestine is more formal and suggests secret planning, often illegal, while covert focuses on being concealed from view.
Secret is the everyday word and works in any context, while covert implies deliberate concealment for a purpose, often in official or strategic settings.

examples.everyday: She gave me a covert wink so the boss wouldn't notice we were leaving early.
examples.professional: The security team flagged several covert login attempts from an unknown account.
examples.analytical: Covert surveillance raises serious questions about privacy, consent, and democratic accountability.

nuance.analogy: A covert operation is like a hidden door behind a bookshelf: it is there, but only the people who know where to push can use it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French covert, the past participle of covrir 'to cover,' from Latin cooperire.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'covert' with 'covet,' which means to desire something strongly and is pronounced differently.
Stressing the second syllable (koh-VERT) instead of the first.

covert.etymology: From Middle English *covert*, from Old French *covert*, past participle of *covrir* (“to cover”) (corresponding to Latin *coopertus*); cognate to *cover*.

senses.definition: Characterized by or related to cupidity (greed, desire for wealth).

core.definition: Greedy or strongly desiring wealth or possessions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -PID-. The ending -ous is pronounced like us, and the final syllable is unstressed and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting excessive greed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word in conversation. It appears in old literature, sermons or academic writing on ethics. In everyday speech, say greedy or grasping.

distinctions.note: Greedy is the common everyday word; cupidinous is rare and more literary.
Avaricious is also formal and emphasizes love of money; cupidinous is broader and more old-fashioned.

examples.professional: The executive's cupidinous approach to bonuses alienated the entire engineering team.
examples.analytical: The moralist condemns the cupidinous ruler who sacrifices the common good for private gain.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand that closes over everything it touches and never opens.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cupidus, desirous, from cupere, to desire.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with cupid, the god of love
Using it in casual speech where greedy is more natural

senses.definition: Extreme greed, especially for wealth.

core.definition: Intense greed, especially a strong desire for money or wealth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -PID-. The final -ity is a short ih sound followed by a long ee, so do not pronounce it as a separate ih and t.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting moral fault.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cupidity mainly in formal writing, news commentary or ethics discussions. It is rarely used in casual conversation, where greed is preferred. It sounds elevated, so use it deliberately in a sentence about corruption or moral failure.

distinctions.note: Greed is the everyday word; cupidity is more formal and often used in moral or literary contexts.
Avarice is formal and focuses on hoarding money; cupidity covers any intense desire for gain.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the cupidity of those people who bought every ticket just to resell them makes me angry.
examples.professional: Our risk review flagged the cupidity of the sales team that pushed for unsafe discounts.
examples.analytical: Hobbes and Augustine both treat cupidity as a root of social conflict, though they explain its origin differently.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that grows hotter the more wood it is given.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cupiditas, desire, from cupidus, desirous.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a long ee sound
Using it as a synonym for curiosity, which is a different meaning

cupidity.etymology: From French *cupidité*, from Latin *cupiditās* (“strong desire”), from *cupidus* (“keen, desirous”).

senses.definition: Discouraging; inspiring fear.
Intimidatingly impressive; awe-inspiring, overwhelming.
Appearing to be difficult; challenging.
senses.example: It was a daunting task, but it was accomplished with some forward planning.

senses.definition: Gerund of daunt.
The act of discouraging or intimidating; discouragement, intimidation.
The act of defeating, overcoming, or overwhelming.

core.definition: Seeming very difficult or intimidating, so that you feel discouraged or unsure you can succeed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ing is a reduced short i, so say it as 'ting' rather than 'teeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on context. It usually signals a serious challenge, but can also describe something impressively large.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say daunting in both casual and professional talk, often about tasks, deadlines or big decisions. It is a bit more formal than hard or tough. A natural reply is to acknowledge the difficulty and offer help or perspective.

distinctions.note: Difficult describes a task's objective hardness, while daunting describes how intimidating it feels to the person facing it.
Challenging is more positive and suggests something worth engaging with, while daunting suggests fear or hesitation.

examples.everyday: Moving to a new city alone sounds daunting, but my friends made it a lot easier.
examples.professional: Migrating our legacy database in one sprint is daunting, so let's split it into smaller milestones.
examples.analytical: The sheer number of variables in the model makes interpretation daunting for anyone without a strong background in statistics.

nuance.analogy: A daunting task is like a mountain trail that looks endless from the trailhead: the view is real, but it makes you hesitate before the first step.
nuance.etymology: From daunt (verb), with the -ing adjective ending.
common_mistakes: Using daunting to mean boring or dull, which it does not mean.
Saying 'I am daunting' instead of 'I am daunted' or 'It is daunting' for the feeling.

core.definition: A town in the hill country of ancient Judah, captured by Joshua and later by Othniel, also called Kiriath-sepher.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DEE. The second syllable is a short 'bih' and the final r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Debir in Bible study, historical geography, or Old Testament commentary. It is not used in everyday speech. When speaking, you can say it is a city in southern Judah in the Hebrew Bible.

distinctions.note: Hebron is a major city near Debir in the same region; Debir is a smaller town in the southern hill country.
Kiriath-sepher is another name for Debir, given in Joshua 15:49.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study group, we were reading about the town of Debir and how Caleb's family took it.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, students compare Joshua's capture of Debir with the later account in Judges.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Debir in Joshua 10 and 15 raises questions about the relation of conquest traditions to Judean settlement history.

nuance.analogy: Debir is like a small mountain stronghold on a map that every Bible reader learns to find.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Debir, uncertain; often linked to a word meaning inner room or sanctuary, though this is disputed.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'dih-BEER'.
Confusing Debir with Dibon, a different town east of the Jordan.
nuance.biblical_note: Debir (Hebrew דְּבִיר) was a city in the southern hill country of Judah, first captured by Joshua, and later taken by Othniel, the son of Kenaz, who won Achsah in marriage. Joshua 10:38-39 describes its capture; Joshua 15:15-16 and Judges 1:11-15 tell of Caleb and Othniel taking it. Joshua 15:49 gives its alternative name, Kiriath-sepher.

senses.definition: Becoming gradually less; diminishing.
Waning.
senses.example: a decrescent moon

senses.definition: A crescent oriented with horns turned to sinister (pointing to the viewer's right).

core.definition: Gradually becoming smaller or less; waning, as the moon does after it is full.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KREH. The final syllable is a reduced ent, and the s is a plain s sound, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use decrescent outside astronomy, literature, or heraldry. In everyday speech, they would say waning or getting smaller. The heraldic sense of decrescent, a crescent with horns pointing toward the viewer's right, is specialized and seldom used except by experts.

distinctions.note: Waning is the common English word for a shrinking moon or fading power; decrescent is more technical and literary.
Decreasing is a general word for going down in amount; decrescent suggests a gradual, graceful reduction, usually of light.
A crescent is a shape; a decrescent is a shape or phase that is getting smaller.

examples.everyday: The moon looks decrescent tonight, so it will be a thin sliver by the weekend.
examples.professional: The telescope log notes a decrescent phase of the moon during the observation window.
examples.analytical: The poet uses the decrescent moon as an image of mortal hope, which fades but is never fully extinguished.

nuance.analogy: A decrescent moon is like a candle burning down slowly: each night there is a little less of it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin decrescere, 'to decrease,' from de- plus crescere, 'to grow.'
common_mistakes: Confusing decrescent with decrepit, which means worn out.
Using decrescent for things that suddenly disappear; it implies a gradual process.

decrescent.etymology: From *decressant*, from Anglo-Norman, present participle of *decreistre* (“to decrease”).

senses.definition: To cook (food) by deep-frying.
To alter a photograph using filters and image compression to make it appear strangely colored for a humorous effect.
senses.example: That meme is deep-fried, which is what makes it so funny.

senses.definition: A heated cooking pan or appliance used to deep-fry foods.

core.definition: To cook food by submerging it completely in hot oil until it is crisp and golden.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'fry', the second part of the word, and the 'ee' in 'deep' is long. Keep the r in 'fry' and avoid making it 'fri'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; describes a cooking method, though it may suggest rich or unhealthy food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'deep-fry' for submerging food in oil, as in 'deep-fried turkey' at Thanksgiving or 'deep-fried pickles' at restaurants. It is a common cooking term at home and in restaurants. Americans usually add 'deep' to distinguish it from 'pan-fry' or 'stir-fry'.

distinctions.note: 'Fry' can mean cooking in a little oil in a pan; 'deep-fry' means submerging food in a large amount of hot oil.
Pan-frying uses a shallow layer of oil in a pan; deep-frying uses enough oil to fully cover the food.
Sauté means quickly cooking food in a little fat over high heat; it is not submerged.

examples.everyday: We're going to deep-fry the turkey on Thanksgiving, so make sure the yard is clear.
examples.professional: The kitchen is testing whether we can deep-fry the frozen appetizers without losing crispness on the line.
examples.analytical: Food historians have traced how deep-frying spread across American diners after the arrival of industrial vegetable oils.

nuance.analogy: To deep-fry is to give food a hot oil bath, like a swim in a pool of heat that seals the outside quickly.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'deep' (Old English 'dēop') and 'fry' (from Latin 'frigere', to fry).
common_mistakes: Saying 'deep fry' with two equal stresses; in the verb it is usually written and said as one word with the stress on 'fry'.
Confusing 'deep-fry' with 'fry deep', which is not idiomatic.

conversation.text: They deep-fry the turkey every Thanksgiving.
At the state fair, they deep-fry everything, even butter.
Deep-fry the fries twice to make them extra crispy.

senses.definition: The term (word or phrase) defined in a definition (whether inside a sentence, as a dictionary entry, or otherwise).

core.definition: The word or phrase that is being defined in a definition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EN, the third syllable. The final syllable is a reduced "um," and the plural is "definienda."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "definiendum" almost only in logic, philosophy, and linguistics classes or papers. In everyday speech, people would just say "the word being defined." Use it in academic writing when the distinction between the term and its definition matters.

distinctions.note: The "definiendum" is the term being defined, while the "definiens" is the phrase that does the defining.
"Term" is a general word for any word or phrase with a specific meaning. "Definiendum" refers only to the item under definition.

examples.everyday: When I explain a word to my kid, the word we're talking about is the definiendum and my explanation is the definiens.
examples.professional: In our requirements document, each definiendum must have exactly one definiens to avoid conflicting specifications.
examples.analytical: A circular definition occurs when the definiendum reappears within its own definiens, so the definition fails to give any independent content.

nuance.analogy: A definiendum is like a locked box and the definiens is the key that opens it to show what is inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin definiendum, the gerundive of definire, "to limit, to define," meaning "that which is to be defined."
common_mistakes: Confusing "definiendum" with "definiens" and swapping their roles.
Using the word in casual speech, where it sounds overly technical.

senses.definition: The act of reducing in rank, character, or reputation, or of abasing; a lowering from one's standing or rank in office or society.
The state of being reduced in rank, character, or reputation; baseness; moral, physical, or intellectual degeneracy; disgrace; abasement; debasement.
Diminution or reduction of strength, efficacy, or value; degeneration; deterioration.
A deleterious change in the chemical structure, physical properties or appearance of a material from natural or artificial exposure.
The state or condition of a species or group which exhibits degraded forms; degeneration.
Arrest of development, or degeneration of any organ, or of the body as a whole.
senses.example: muscle degradation

senses.definition: The gradual breakdown of components of a material, as a result of a natural element, i.e.: heat, cold and wind.
A gradual wearing down or wasting, as of rocks and banks, by the action of water, frost etc.

core.definition: The process of losing quality, strength, or value, or a state of moral or social decline, dishonor, or humiliation.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on DAY, with a secondary stress on DEG. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick ruh, and the final -tion is pronounced shun.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes harmful decline, loss of quality, or disgrace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use degradation in science, environmental writing, law, and formal discussions of morality or dignity. In everyday speech, people say decline, damage, wear and tear, or breakdown. A natural sentence is 'Environmental degradation is a serious concern.'

distinctions.note: Deterioration is a general word for becoming worse, while degradation often implies a loss of quality, dignity, or chemical or environmental structure.
Degeneration usually describes biological or structural decline over time, while degradation can describe environmental, moral, or chemical breakdown.

examples.everyday: The old boat has suffered so much salt water degradation that it barely floats.
examples.professional: We are tracking the degradation of response times across the production servers.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the moral degradation of a society that tolerates cruelty as normal.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandcastle slowly eroding under waves until its shape is lost.
nuance.etymology: From Latin degradatio, from degradare, to reduce in rank, from de- (down) and gradus (step).
common_mistakes: Using degradation only for physical wear. It can also refer to moral dignity, rank, or reputation.
Confusing the noun with the verb. Say the degradation of the system, not the system degradation.

senses.definition: To remove a sense of personal identity or individual character from something; to anonymize.
To present (something) as an impersonal object.
To suffer an episode of depersonalization.
senses.example: He's depersonalizing right now, so he's considering checking himself into the hospital.

core.definition: To remove the human or individual character from something, so that people or things are treated as impersonal objects or numbers.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUR, the second syllable. Keep the r strong and rhotic, and do not turn the middle syllables into a clear ee sound; they are reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes something cold or dehumanizing, such as bureaucracy, treatment of patients, or customer service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing about institutions, health care, the workplace, or technology, often with a critical tone. In everyday speech they would say make it feel impersonal or treat people like numbers. In psychology, depersonalization is a clinical term for a feeling of detachment from oneself, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Dehumanize is stronger and implies treating people as less than human; depersonalize is milder and means removing individual identity.
Anonymize means removing identifying information from data; depersonalize can be broader, covering the feel of a system or interaction, not just the data.
Impersonal is an adjective describing a quality; depersonalize is a verb describing the act of making something impersonal.

examples.everyday: I hate how the bank tries to depersonalize everything, so I always ask for the same teller by name.
examples.professional: If we automate every support reply, we risk depersonalizing the customer experience and losing the trust we have built.
examples.analytical: Bureaucratic procedures often depersonalize individuals by reducing them to case numbers, which makes the moral claims of each person easy to ignore.

nuance.analogy: Like taking the name tags off a team uniform, so everyone looks the same and no one is recognized as an individual.
nuance.etymology: From de- ('remove'), personal, and -ize.
common_mistakes: Confusing depersonalize with depersonalization as a clinical symptom without context
Stressing the first syllable as DEE-pur-suh-nize instead of dee-PUR-suh-nuh-lighz

senses.definition: Under the United States Code of Military Justice, a person who has been placed on AWOL status for more than 30 days.
One who is familiar with the desert climate and environment.
A person who has physically removed him- or herself from the control or direction of a military or naval unit with the intention of permanently leaving.

core.definition: A soldier or sailor who leaves military service without permission, intending never to return.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ZUR. The final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so the word ends in a soft, unstressed er sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies disloyalty or cowardice, especially in military or historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deserter for soldiers who leave their units without permission, a serious offense under military law. The military term AWOL, absent without leave, is used for shorter absences. In everyday talk the word can also describe someone who abandons a group or cause, but this is less common.

distinctions.note: AWOL refers to an unauthorized absence, which may be brief. Deserter is used for someone who leaves with the intention of not returning.
A defector switches sides or leaves a country or organization for political reasons. A deserter simply leaves his or her duty.

examples.everyday: My grandfather said he would never call a soldier a deserter unless the man really left his unit for good.
examples.professional: The base reported that two deserters had not returned, so the military police opened an investigation.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the deserter should be judged as a coward or as a person who refused to continue an unjust war.

nuance.analogy: Like a player who walks off the field during the final game, a deserter abandons the team at the moment it needs him most.
nuance.etymology: From desert, from Latin deserere (to leave, forsake).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as DEZ-ur, which puts the stress in the wrong place.
Confusing deserter with desert, the noun for a dry region.

deserter.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *desertor* (“deserter”), from *desero* (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from *desert* + *er*.

senses.definition: Lacking something; devoid.
Lacking money, poor, impoverished; especially, extremely so.
To impoverish; to strip of wealth, resources, etc.

core.definition: Having no money, property or basic necessities; extremely poor.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, DES. The final syllable rhymes with 'loot', not 'choot'. Do not add a 'ch' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative and serious. It describes severe poverty and hardship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use destitute in news, charity appeals and serious discussions of poverty. In everyday speech they would more often say broke, flat broke or really poor. Destitute is stronger than poor; it means having almost nothing.

distinctions.note: Poor is general and everyday; destitute means extremely poor, with no resources at all.
Impoverished emphasizes the process of becoming poor; destitute describes the state of having nothing.
Needy describes a need for help; destitute describes a more severe lack of money or necessities.

examples.everyday: After the flood, my neighbor's family was left destitute, so we brought them food every week.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit provides emergency housing for destitute families who have lost their jobs.
examples.analytical: The author describes the destitute peasants as a class excluded from both property and political participation.

nuance.analogy: Being destitute is like arriving at a table with an empty plate and nothing left in your pockets to buy a meal.
nuance.etymology: From Latin destitutus, 'forsaken, abandoned', past participle of destituere, 'to leave alone, abandon'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'choot' because of the 'tute' spelling.
Using destitute for mild lack of money, when the word means nearly total poverty.

senses.definition: The doctrine that all actions are determined by the current state and immutable laws of the universe, with no possibility of choice.
The property of having behavior determined only by initial state and input.

core.definition: The philosophical view that every event, including human choices, is fully caused by earlier events and natural laws.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TUR in the second syllable and say the final -ism as um, not izm. Keep the middle syllables short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in philosophy and science, though it can carry a negative tone when linked to fatalism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use determinism mostly in philosophy, religion, physics, and debates about free will. In everyday speech they would not use it except when discussing a serious question about whether our choices are predetermined. In software contexts it means that a program always gives the same output for the same input.

distinctions.note: Fatalism says events will happen regardless of what we do; determinism says events are caused by prior causes, which may include our own choices.
Free will is the belief that people can really choose among options; determinism denies this in its strong forms.

examples.everyday: My roommate and I got into a long debate about whether free will is an illusion or whether determinism is true.
examples.professional: Our simulation keeps determinism in the code, so the same input always produces the same result.
examples.analytical: Determinism threatens moral responsibility unless one can show that compatibilist freedom is still meaningful.

nuance.analogy: Determinism is like a row of dominoes: each fall is caused by the one before, so the whole chain is set once the first domino is pushed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin determinare, to limit or define, with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using determinism when the word fatalism is meant, which implies inevitability regardless of cause.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a strong vowel, saying dih-TUR-meh-nizm.

senses.definition: To ruin many or all things over a large area, such as most or all buildings of a city, or cities of a region, or trees of a forest.
To destroy a whole collection of related ideas, beliefs, and strongly held opinions.
To break beyond recovery or repair so that the only options are abandonment or the clearing away of useless remains (if any) and starting over.
To greatly demoralize, to cause to suffer intense grief or dismay.

core.definition: To cause great destruction to a place, or to hurt someone so badly emotionally that they are shaken for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, so say DEV-uh-stayt, not de-VAS-tate. Many learners stretch the middle vowel into a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes severe damage or deep emotional harm, so it is strong and should not be used for minor problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use devastate for disasters such as hurricanes, fires, or floods, and in news reports about wars. In everyday talk it often appears in the passive, as in 'We were devastated by the news,' which is more common than the active form for personal hurt. Using it for a small inconvenience, like a late bus, sounds exaggerated.

distinctions.note: Destroy is the general word for ruining something completely; devastate adds a sense of widespread damage over a large area or a deep emotional blow.
Ruin can apply to a single object, plan, or reputation in a neutral way, while devastate is stronger and suggests overwhelming impact.

examples.everyday: The tornado devastated our neighborhood, so we're staying with my sister until the houses are rebuilt.
examples.professional: The outage devastated our reporting pipeline, so we need a plan to restore the data before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: Such a theology, if taken seriously, would devastate the moral foundations on which the community's claims about justice rest.

nuance.analogy: A flood that sweeps through a town leaves nothing standing where it passed, like a fire that burns a forest to ash.
nuance.etymology: From Latin devastare, 'to lay waste', from de- (completely) and vastare (to make desolate).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (de-VAS-tate) instead of the first.
Using devastate for minor disappointments, which sounds dramatic to Americans.

devastate.etymology: Latin *dēvastātus*, perfect passive participle of *dēvastō* (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see *-ate*); from *dē-* + *vastō* (“to destroy, lay waste”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to dialogue.
(Of a literary work) written in dialogue.
Of or relating to dialogism.
senses.example: Intertextuality is concerned with dialogic literature.

core.definition: Relating to dialogue, or written as a conversation between speakers, or relating to dialogism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH, the second main syllable. The final -ic is 'ik', and the 'g' is a soft 'j' sound, as in 'jam'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a feature of communication or writing without evaluating it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dialogic in literary criticism, education, and communication theory, as in 'dialogic teaching' or 'dialogic learning.' In casual speech they would say 'conversational' or 'back-and-forth.' Be careful: dialogic and dialectic are different words, and dialogic does not mean argumentative.

distinctions.note: Dialogic refers to dialogue as a form or mode of communication; dialectic is a method of reasoning through contradiction.
Conversational is the everyday word for relaxed talk; dialogic is more technical and often refers to an approach or structure of discussion.

examples.everyday: Our book club is pretty dialogic, since everyone builds on each other's comments.
examples.professional: We switched the training to a dialogic format, so new hires ask questions throughout the session.
examples.analytical: Bakhtin's novels are dialogic, because their meaning emerges from the clash of many distinct voices.

nuance.analogy: A dialogic text is like a potluck: each voice brings a different dish, and the meal depends on all of them.
nuance.etymology: From dialogue, from Greek dialogos, 'conversation,' with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Confusing dialogic with dialectic and assuming it means argumentative reasoning.
Saying 'DYE-uh-LOH-jik' with a long o, which is not the standard American pronunciation.

dialogic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *διαλογικός* (“related to a dialogue”), from *διάλογος* (“conversation, discourse, dialogue”), equivalent to *dialog* + *-ic*.

senses.definition: The act of dilating.
State of being dilated; expansion; dilatation.
In morphology, a basic operation (denoted ⊕) that usually uses a structuring element for probing and expanding the shapes contained in the input image.

core.definition: The process of becoming wider or larger, such as a pupil, blood vessel, or cervix.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAY. The -tion ending is pronounced like 'shun', and the first syllable sounds like 'dy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term used in medicine, optics, and mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dilation mainly in medical settings, such as pupil dilation at an eye exam or cervical dilation during childbirth. In mathematics and image processing it names a specific operation. In everyday speech people more often say the pupils got bigger or the eyes opened wider.

distinctions.note: Expansion is a general increase in size; dilation specifically refers to widening, often of an opening or tube-like structure.
Dilatation is a less common variant spelling used mostly in British and older medical writing; Americans usually choose dilation.

examples.everyday: The eye doctor put drops in my eyes to cause dilation so she could look at the back of my eye.
examples.professional: In our image pipeline, dilation expands the bright regions of the mask by one pixel to fill small gaps.
examples.analytical: The mathematical operation of dilation is defined by translating a structuring element across the set and taking the union of the results.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a door wider to let more people through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dilatatio, from dilatare, to spread out, from dis- apart and latus, wide.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of LAY.
Using dilation to describe delaying, which is the meaning of dilatory.

senses.definition: In a diligent manner, with appropriate effort, carefully.

core.definition: In a careful, steady way, putting in consistent effort to do something well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is reduced to a light 'lee'. Non-native speakers often add an extra vowel between the 'l' and 'j' or stress the 'ent' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises careful, persistent effort and is often used in evaluations, school reports, and job reviews.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word more in writing, reviews, and formal speech than in casual talk. In conversation people more often say 'carefully' or 'hard' or 'really working on it.' It works well in a performance review or a thank-you note, for example 'She diligently checked every number.'

distinctions.note: Carefully focuses on avoiding mistakes; diligently adds the idea of sustained, persistent effort over time.
Hard describes intensity of effort; diligently suggests steady, conscientious work, often over a long period.

examples.everyday: My daughter studies diligently every night before her driving test.
examples.professional: Our QA team diligently checked every dataset before the model was released.
examples.analytical: The text urges believers to labor diligently in the study of Scripture rather than rely on quick impressions.

nuance.analogy: Think of a gardener who weeds a little every day rather than once a year; diligence is steady, patient attention.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diligere, 'to esteem highly, love,' from di- and legere, 'choose, pick out.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'i' in the first syllable (it is short, /ɪ/).
Using 'diligently' for a single quick action; it describes sustained care.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the idea is linked to ḥārûṣ, 'sharp, diligent,' from a root meaning to be keen or quick; in Greek, spoudazō means to be eager and make haste. Proverbs 10:4 and 13:4 (RSV) contrast the diligent hand, which gains prosperity, with the slack hand and the sluggard. Deuteronomy 6:7 (RSV) tells parents to teach God's commandments diligently to their children. In 2 Timothy 2:15 (RSV) Paul urges Timothy to do his best to present himself as one approved, a worker who handles the word of truth well.

senses.definition: To render unable; to take away an ability of, as by crippling.
To impair the physical or mental abilities of; to cause a serious, permanent injury.
senses.example: Falling off the horse disabled him.

senses.definition: To deactivate, to make inoperational (especially of a function of an electronic or mechanical device).
senses.example: The pilot had to disable the autopilot of his airplane.

core.definition: To turn off or stop a feature, device, or program from working, or to make a person physically or mentally unable to do something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, AY. The final syllable is weak, so say it as bul, not bl. The first syllable is short, like the i in sit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for devices and software; negative or sensitive for people, where disability and person with a disability are preferred.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, disable is used for turning off software features, alarms, or devices, as in 'Disable the pop-up blocker.' For people, Americans avoid saying disabled people as a description; they say people with disabilities. Use the verb for people only in technical or legal contexts.

distinctions.note: Enable means to make a feature or ability active; disable means the opposite, to turn it off or stop it.
Impair means to weaken something, and it is often used for abilities or judgment; disable is stronger and suggests stopping a function or capacity completely.

examples.everyday: Can you disable the alarm before you open the back door? It goes off every time I walk in.
examples.professional: We should disable the old login endpoint before the migration, so no one can use it by accident.
examples.analytical: To disable a moral faculty is not the same as to deny it; the argument depends on which sense of disable the author intends.

nuance.analogy: Disable is like pulling the fuse on a circuit: the power is still in the system, but it no longer flows through that part.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (reversal) and able, from Latin habilis, handy or fit.
common_mistakes: Describing people as disabled in the sense of incapacitated, when Americans prefer people with disabilities
Using disable with a person object in casual speech, where turn off is more natural for devices

senses.definition: Freedom from passion; the absence of passion; an undisturbed state; ataraxy.

core.definition: Freedom from strong emotion or passion; a calm, undisturbed state of mind, especially in philosophy and spiritual writing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on DIS, with a lighter stress on PASH. The ending -tion is pronounced shun, with a reduced final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in philosophy and spiritual writing; it can sound cold in ordinary speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in daily life. You will meet it in philosophy, religious writing and literary description of calm detachment. In everyday speech say calm or composure instead.

distinctions.note: Apathy is lack of interest or concern; dispassion is calm freedom from emotional distortion while still caring about truth.
Detachment means separation from involvement; dispassion specifically means freedom from emotion or bias.
Calm is an everyday word for a relaxed state; dispassion is more technical and focuses on the absence of passion.

examples.everyday: She listened to the argument with a quiet dispassion that annoyed her brother.
examples.professional: Our reviewers evaluated the proposals with dispassion, setting aside personal preferences.
examples.analytical: In the desert fathers' writing, dispassion is pursued not as coldness but as a clarity that frees the heart for love.

nuance.analogy: Like still water, where you can see the bottom clearly because nothing is churning it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin dispassio, from Latin dis- 'not' plus passio 'suffering, emotion'.
common_mistakes: Using the noun where the adjective dispassionate is needed; say a dispassionate tone, not a dispassion tone.
Treating it as a synonym for indifference or boredom, which changes the meaning completely.

senses.definition: Physical or emotional discomfort, suffering, or alarm, particularly of a more acute nature.
A cause of such discomfort.
Serious danger.
senses.example: a ship in distress

senses.definition: A seizing of property without legal process to force payment of a debt.
The thing taken by distraining; that which is seized to procure satisfaction.
An aversive state of stress to which a person cannot fully adapt.
To cause strain or anxiety to someone.
To retain someone’s property against the payment of a debt; to distrain.
To treat a new object to give it an appearance of age.
senses.example: a pair of distressed jeans

core.definition: Extreme anxiety, pain or sorrow, often a sign that someone needs help.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, so say dih-STRESS, not DIS-tress. The vowel is the short e of bed, and the final s is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes suffering or alarm. In technical contexts like maritime distress it is a neutral signal of emergency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'in distress' for someone who needs help, and 'a distress call' or 'distress signal' for emergencies. In everyday conversation you can say 'He's in a lot of distress about his job.' Do not confuse it with stress, which is more common for everyday pressure. A distress call is serious, so use it only for real emergencies.

distinctions.note: Stress is usually milder, everyday pressure, while distress implies greater pain or alarm.
Anguish is an intense, prolonged suffering, usually deeper than distress.
Worry is a mild, often anticipatory concern, while distress is a stronger state of being upset.

examples.everyday: She was in real distress after she got the call from the hospital.
examples.professional: The schedule change is causing the team a lot of distress, so let's talk about the timeline.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard treats despair as a distress the self cannot easily name, which is why it hides from itself.

nuance.analogy: Distress is like a smoke alarm going off in your mind: it is loud, unpleasant and a signal that something needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From Old French destresse, from Latin distringere, to draw apart or hinder.
common_mistakes: Confusing distress with stress and using them as interchangeable in serious contexts.
Stressing the first syllable as DIS-tress.
Using distress for ordinary tiredness, which is too strong.
nuance.biblical_note: In Romans 8:35 Paul lists distress among the trials that cannot separate believers from the love of Christ; the Greek word is stenochoria, literally narrowness of space, meaning a cramped or pressed situation. In Luke 21:25 Jesus speaks of distress among nations in the last days, a sense of anxious bewilderment in the face of cosmic signs. Both passages describe suffering as something that Scripture does not treat as the final word.

senses.definition: A property of functions that have a rule describing how the function can be performed to the individual components of another operation.
senses.example: If function f is distributive with respect to function g, then f(a,g(b,c))=g(f(a,b),f(a,c)).

senses.definition: Relating to distribution.
Tending to distribute; serving to divide and assign in portions; dealing a proper share to each.
Assigning the species of a general term.
Expressing separation; denoting a taking singly, not collectively.
senses.example: a distributive adjective or pronoun, such as "each", "either", or "every"

senses.definition: Distributive case.
A distributive adjective or pronoun.
A distributive numeral.

core.definition: Describing a property where an operation on a sum equals the sum of the operation applied to each part, such as a(b+c)=ab+ac.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STRIB, not on the first syllable. The middle vowels reduce to a schwa, so do not pronounce the u as a full oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a neutral term used in mathematics and occasionally in philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the distributive property in school math when they talk about multiplying across addition, for example 3 times 12 equals 3 times 10 plus 3 times 2. In philosophy, distributive justice means fair sharing of resources. The British term is often distributive law, but American classrooms use distributive property.

distinctions.note: Distributive describes an algebraic rule, while distributional describes how data is spread.
Collective refers to a group as a whole, while distributive refers to properties applied to each individual part.
Associative describes how grouping does not change the result, while distributive describes how multiplication interacts with addition.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked why 3 times 12 works when you split it up, and I told her it's the distributive property.
examples.professional: In the symbolic library, we rely on the distributive property to expand the expression before simplifying.
examples.analytical: Distributivity lets multiplication interact coherently with addition, which is why a ring requires it as an axiom.
